inline.s: “When thought is just arising, one does not see that there is any thought to arise: this is called no-thought. It is not as ordinary people imagine, that the absence of a single thought arising is what is meant by no-thought.”

The so-called no-thought does not mean that not a single thought arises; it means that even though thoughts arise, one does not abide in them, does not linger in them. The no-thought that ordinary people imagine — “not a single thought arising” — is merely suppressing thoughts so that they do not arise. They think that having no thoughts at all is good practice. In fact, one is dead there, and far from attaining the Way, one has earned a place among clods of earth and stones! Have you not heard the case of the Sixth Patriarch saving Chan Master Wolun? Wolun at first thought that suppressing thoughts so that none arose was good practice, and so he had a verse: “Wolun has a device: he can cut off the hundred thoughts; facing states, his mind does not arise; bodhi grows day by day.” The Sixth Patriarch saw that he had entered a dead end, and so he saved him: “Huineng has no device; he does not cut off the hundred thoughts; facing states, his mind arises again and again — how does bodhi grow?” To raise the mind is just not to raise the mind; to stir a thought is just not to stir a thought — the Sixth Patriarch abided in nothing! “Facing states, his mind arises again and again” means the wondrous function arises. If one did not raise the mind or stir a thought, one would be dead there — what wondrous function could still arise? Could one still expound the Dharma for people? No. Bodhi is simply the self-nature: it is neither born nor extinguished, neither defiled nor pure, neither increasing nor decreasing. In an ordinary being it is not diminished — even in hell it is not less; in a sage it is not increased — even at Buddhahood it is not more. Long ago someone asked a great Chan master: What is it like after enlightenment? The master answered: Not a fraction is added. He asked again: And before enlightenment? He answered: Not a fraction is subtracted. So Wolun was wrong when he said “bodhi grows day by day.”

“Relying on deluded thoughts, one tunes and cultivates the dharma-body; then all deluded thoughts that appear are tuned and manifested as the self-nature’s wondrous enjoyment. That is to say, even the coarse deluded thoughts manifested by the five poisons can all be made to possess the luminous power of the self-nature’s liberation, and clarity-emptiness becomes enjoyment.”

To tune and cultivate the dharma-body by relying on the arising and ceasing of deluded thoughts means that when a deluded thought arises, one awakens at once, recognizes it, and does not run after it — it does not mean pressing deluded thoughts to death so that they do not move. It means awakening at every moment, illuminating at every moment, not running after deluded thoughts. If you run after deluded thoughts and become attached to states, then you are lost. This is why the Pure Land school stresses reciting the Buddha-name at every moment — not to make you greedy for more, greedy for the mark of merit, but to make you awaken, recognize the dharma-body, and protect the dharma-body. In our practice we must work right on deluded thoughts; there is no second way. Reciting the Buddha-name, holding mantras, or investigating Chan — the aim of all of them is to tune and govern these deluded thoughts. So to rely on deluded thoughts to tune and cultivate the dharma-body is to work on deluded thoughts, cutting them off and not letting them continue without cease. All Buddhadharma is the tuning and cultivation of the dharma-body; all of it is work on deluded thoughts. Do not do Buddha-recitation as a form-bound merit — that is a mistake. Therefore Master Lianchi said: “Voice after voice awakens the master within.” Buddha-recitation is awakening the master within, making you realize.

If you know how to work on deluded thoughts and, relying on deluded thoughts, tune and cultivate the dharma-body, then “all deluded thoughts that appear are tuned and manifested as the self-nature’s wondrous enjoyment; that is to say, even the coarse deluded thoughts manifested by the five poisons can all be made to possess the luminous power of the self-nature’s liberation, and clarity-emptiness becomes enjoyment.” Then all the deluded thoughts that arise are tuned into the subtle enjoyment of the manifest self-nature; even the coarse deluded thoughts manifested by the five poisons of form, feeling, conception, formations, and consciousness can all be made to possess the power and light of the self-nature’s liberation, and one enters the realm of luminous emptiness. In other words, one can transform the poisons of the five aggregates into the self-nature’s wondrous enjoyment, making them the tools of our practice and realization and the provisions for Buddhahood.

If we tune our own minds well — not abiding in marks, not abiding in states, not afflicted — we obtain great enjoyment. Wondrous enjoyment means subtle enjoyment, most enjoyable. To obtain enjoyment is very good, but to crave indulgence is ruinous. “Enjoyment” and “indulgence” differ by a single word, yet the difference is vast — as far apart as heaven and earth. If you are particular about eating well and dressing well, dating the opposite sex, dancing, going to the movies, living amid wine and bright lights, sunk in luxury and pleasure, and then, once these conditions are gone, commit crimes to reach your pleasures — that is ruinous; that is craving indulgence. But if at all times the mind is empty and unattached, peaceful and at ease, never chasing outer states, content with only gruel to eat today, indifferent to living in a broken thatched hut, broad-minded, at peace with reason, content and always happy, at ease with conditions — that is wondrous enjoyment. Know how to work on deluded thoughts and tune your self-nature well, and you will naturally obtain wondrous enjoyment: “A single mind of equanimity, and all vanishes of itself.” A mind of equanimity is a mind with not the slightest crookedness — level, straight, and frank. “All vanishes of itself” means the mind is utterly empty, without a speck of affliction. How beautiful this is! So learning the Buddhadharma is to obtain great enjoyment and open great wisdom. Learning the Buddhadharma is not seeking anything; to have something to seek is ruinous. To seek blessings and rewards, to seek superknowledges — that is not learning the Buddhadharma; to seek wealth, to seek office — even less so. Everything is false, like flowers in the sky, like the moon in water; in the end all is emptiness! So we must at every moment recognize the true mind, rely on deluded thoughts to tune and cultivate the dharma-body, and not let deluded thoughts cover the true mind. Recognize that deluded thoughts are the wondrous function arising from the true mind; thus not abiding in marks, you will obtain true enjoyment and no affliction will arise. And the reverse? If you do not know how to rely on deluded thoughts to tune and cultivate the dharma-body, then afflictions are endless and the gully of desire can never be filled. Having a hundred, you want a thousand; having a thousand, you want ten thousand; having ten thousand, you want tens of millions, hundreds of millions — there is never a moment of satisfaction, and affliction and suffering have no end.
“All deluded thoughts are the wondrous function arising within the self-nature’s all-penetrating state.”

This explains still further the arising of deluded thoughts. Deluded thoughts are indeed produced by the true mind, but without the conditions of states they could not arise either. The conditions of states are “the self-nature’s all-penetrating state.” We have said again and again above that sun, moon, and stars, mountains, rivers, and the great earth, self and others, sentient beings, flowers, birds, insects, and fish are all manifested by the self-nature. But if the conditions of states are the same for all ordinary beings, why are they of so many different kinds? Because the nature of karma makes them so. Ordinary beings do not recognize the self-nature, and so they are deluded. Because of delusion they create karma; because of karma they receive retribution. Shared karma manifests mountains, rivers, and the great earth; individual karma manifests the twelve classes of beings. As their causes of good and evil differ, so the states they manifest differ. All these different states are felt and penetrated within the self-nature and understood within the self-nature; they have no substantial reality, they are false and unreal. As for the self-nature itself, cause is within it and effect is within it. The self-nature transcends cause and effect; all the different states are “the self-nature’s all-penetrating state,” which is what is called “the objective aspect of the eighth consciousness.” And “the subjective aspect of the eighth consciousness” in turn discriminates and chooses among “objective aspects,” and this discriminating and choosing is what is called “deluded thought.” It is one and the same eighth consciousness — the ālaya-consciousness: deluded, it is the eighth consciousness; awakened, it is the “tathāgatagarbha mind.” Therefore, if one can “rely on deluded thoughts to tune and cultivate the dharma-body” — returning from delusion to awakening — then “all deluded thoughts are the wondrous function arising within the self-nature’s all-penetrating state.” Deluded thoughts are the wondrous function arising from the true mind!
“Protect it with a mind that neither grasps nor rejects, because its arising and ceasing cannot transcend the realm of the dharma-body’s wondrous-function king.”

As the name suggests, “deluded thoughts” are thoughts that are false and unreal. Because they discriminate and choose among false and unreal outer states, their “discriminating and choosing” is likewise false and unreal. But though deluded thoughts are “deluded,” they are the wondrous function of the true mind. Once you have recognized the true mind, you must “protect it” well. To protect is to guard; to maintain is to keep up — guard it well and maintain its position of “being master.” That is why the true mind is also called “the master within.” How do you protect it? “Protect it with a mind that neither grasps nor rejects” — you must protect the true mind by neither grasping nor rejecting outer states. Toward all outer states, do not raise a discriminating mind: this thing is good, I must get it; that thing is bad, I must abandon it. Do not have a mind of love and hate, of grasping and rejecting; take away this mind of love and hate, of grasping and rejecting — that is protecting the true mind. The reason we fail to attain liberation is that we are ruined precisely by “love, hate, grasping, and rejecting.” Oh! How fine this gold is — I must get it into my hands! This place is no good — hurry and get far away from it.

Speaking of this, I recall a modern case. There was a Dharma master in Hangzhou who said: “Though not a few people expound the Diamond Sutra, a single sentence can stump them all. The Diamond Sutra says there is no mark of person, no mark of self, no mark of purity, no mark of defilement. Well then, here is a heap of dung — you have no marks, so eat it up!” This is not challenging those who expound the Diamond Sutra; it is challenging the very meaning of the sutra! In fact his question is easy to answer. Answer him: “Please hold it in your mouth and bring it here.” Did you not tell me to eat it? Then please take it up in your mouth and bring it over! That is the polite answer. If one is not polite, then shout at him: “Hey! You, a Dharma master, have been buried by a heap of dung.” He saw that heap of dung and became attached to its mark — which is to be buried by the dung. All of this is the mischief of a mind of love and hate, grasping and rejecting! Therefore we must not raise a mind of love and hate, of grasping and rejecting, toward outer states; this is protecting the true mind.

Why must we protect the true mind in this way? “Because its arising and ceasing cannot transcend the realm of the dharma-body’s wondrous-function king.” Because the arising and ceasing of deluded thoughts cannot transcend the realm of “the dharma-body’s wondrous-function king”! The dharma-body’s wondrous function embraces everything, and so it is called “king.” The arising and ceasing of deluded thoughts is of course also within the realm of “the dharma-body’s wondrous-function king,” not outside the range of the true mind’s wondrous function. Therefore, however much deluded thoughts arise and cease, so long as I do not run after them, am not dragged along by them, am not moved by them, that is protecting the true mind.
“Though deluded thoughts possess the marks of ignorance, their self-nature does not go beyond the purity of the wisdom dharma-body.”

The Heart Sutra says: “He illuminated the five aggregates and saw that they were all empty.” The five aggregates are also called the five shadows: form, feeling, conception, formations, and consciousness. The aggregate of form belongs to form-dharmas, and form-dharmas have marks. Men and women, young and old, mountains, rivers, and the great earth, grasses, trees, and forests are all marks of form. Feeling, conception, formations, and consciousness are mind-dharmas, and mind-dharmas have no marks. Delusive thinking belongs to mind-dharmas — so why is it said that deluded thoughts “possess the marks of ignorance”? To raise a deluded thought is to abide and to grasp. Grasp what? Grasp the false appearance of form-dharmas — grasp the marks of form. The moment a deluded thought arises, there is the shadow of a mark of form in the mind; therefore deluded thoughts “possess the marks of ignorance.” In fact, mind-dharmas are just form-dharmas, and form-dharmas are just mind-dharmas. Apart from the true mind, what second dharma is there? But because of ignorance, the moment a mind-dharma stirs, it becomes the shadow of a form-dharma, and so it is called “the marks of ignorance.” The marks of ignorance are likewise false and unobtainable. If you can “rely on deluded thoughts to tune and cultivate the dharma-body,” then “all deluded thoughts that appear are tuned and manifested as the self-nature’s wondrous enjoyment.” Why can deluded thoughts be turned into wondrous enjoyment? Because “their self-nature does not go beyond the purity of the wisdom dharma-body.”

The “self-nature” spoken of here means “one’s own nature.” The own nature of a deluded thought is false and unreal; one may also say that deluded thoughts have no self-nature, like “flowers in the sky” — like seeing flowers in empty space. That is because the eyes are diseased, because a film has grown over the eye, that one sees flowers in space; in fact there are no flowers in space. A film over the eye is a metaphor for the mind’s delusive thinking and attachment; seeing flowers in space is a metaphor for taking the false as real, for delusively grasping and delusively seizing. This is to be deluded not only about empty space — failing to see true suchness — but also about where the real flowers grow: one cannot understand that deluded thoughts and deluded states are both the true mind’s wondrous function. Ignorance and deluded thoughts are both like “flowers in the sky” (in ancient times the two characters hua and hua were used interchangeably), both without substantial reality, both false. But why can they arise? Because we possess the numinous, luminous true mind! The true mind is like the great ocean; deluded thoughts are like the waves. Without the great ocean there are no waves; without the true mind where would deluded thoughts come from? The true mind is the wisdom dharma-body, and the true mind is originally pure. Therefore the own nature of deluded thoughts does not go beyond “the purity of the wisdom dharma-body.” The Song of Realizing the Way says: “The true nature of ignorance is the Buddha-nature; the illusory empty body is the dharma-body.” The true nature of ignorance is the tathatā Buddha-nature; the “originally empty” body, illusory and magical, is the wisdom dharma-body. For the false body and mind do not go beyond the range of the pure wisdom dharma-body. This is true reality, this is the one true dharma-realm.
“In the illumination of the vast, unbroken light, the self-nature of deluded thoughts is originally empty.”

The vast, unbroken light” — what is it? It is our wisdom dharma-body. The dharma-body is incomparably vast, forever unbroken, and immeasurably luminous. The Buddha Speaks of Amitābha Sutra says: “The light of that Buddha is immeasurable, shining throughout the lands of the ten directions without obstruction. Therefore he is named Amitābha.” Amitābha means Infinite Light and Infinite Life. Infinite Light is the “vastness” of space; Infinite Life is the “unbrokenness” of time; Amitābha is “the vast, unbroken light.” In our practice, whether we recite the Buddha-name, investigate Chan, or cultivate the esoteric teachings, all of it is the cultivation of mind. When the mind is empty and pure, a great light blazes forth. Why does it not blaze forth now? Because ignorance covers it, as a pearl wrapped in mud loses its luster. But though the light is not seen, it is still there! In fact the light has never left us; in daily life — working, writing, inventing, creating — this too is still light, still the dharma-body’s wondrous function, only not fully brought into play. Within the bright illumination of this “vast, unbroken light,” the own nature of all deluded thoughts is originally empty and still.

Do not fear deluded thoughts: when deluded thoughts subside, that is the true mind. If deluded thoughts arise, let them be like drawings on water — drawn and erased at once; do not linger, do not cling. At once give a keen awakening, and with the arising and ceasing they vanish. The Pure Land school raises the Buddha-name, the Chan school raises the doubt-sensation, the esoteric school holds mudrās and mantras — all to transform deluded thoughts and protect the true mind. Practicing thus, closely and continuously, in no more than a few years you will certainly succeed. What is to be feared is that we refuse to do this, refuse to guard it closely and continuously, but let deluded thoughts fly about at random and indulge them, letting them blaze up like a great fire — indulging them until they burn fiercely, and then you cannot succeed. Therefore, so long as you recognize that the self-nature of deluded thoughts is originally empty and do not fear them, they are the true mind’s wondrous function, they are the Way. Reciting the Buddha-name, investigating Chan, cultivating the esoteric teachings — the aim of all is to cut off deluded thoughts and not wander along with them. If there are no “leaking deluded thoughts,” the “karmic cause of transmigration” is cut off.
“If one practices and applies it in long habituation, deluded thoughts will of themselves be tuned and governed; movement and stillness are undivided, and one attains indestructible abiding.”

Morning in it, evening in it, in wanderings in it, in adversity in it — practicing at every moment, never forgetting in any place — this is called “long habituation.” Xing means to practice, actually to do it; chi means to maintain, to keep it up constantly. If one thus “practices and applies it in long habituation,” then “deluded thoughts will of themselves be tuned and governed; movement and stillness are undivided, and one attains indestructible abiding.” To be tuned and governed of themselves means that you need not subdue them; they subdue themselves. Our practice is like herding an ox: at first you must watch and discipline it at every moment, but once it is tamed, you need not watch it and it obeys you. By then, when you want to raise a thought, a thought is raised; when you want no thought, no thought arises. Raising a thought is for use; if it is not needed, no thought arises — that is success in cultivation. Ordinary beings are not masters of their thoughts: when they do not want a thought to arise, it arises anyway, jumping up from the mind of itself — that is why they are called “deluded thoughts.” If a practitioner is the same, then the practice has not been done well, and one must correct one’s understanding and apply effort properly. “Movement and stillness are undivided” means that movement is fine, stillness is fine, sitting in meditation is fine, working is fine — there is no distinction; all is the same. If I tell you to raise a thought, you raise it; if I tell you not to raise a thought, you do not — movement and stillness are one suchness. At the very moment a thought is arising, one does not see where the thought comes from — this is to have no thought arise at any moment, and not to be a dead pool of water with not a single thought, but simply not to abide. Reaching this stage, one “attains indestructible abiding” and will not be destroyed. This physical body of ours will decay and die; when conditions are exhausted the four elements separate — but the dharma-body is not destroyed. To attain indestructible abiding is to accomplish the Way. The Great Mudrā tells us to work on the ground of mind; there is no need to cultivate any other method — directly apply effort on the ground of mind. Illuminate at every moment, like drawing on water, utterly unattached. Practicing thus, in time deluded thoughts are naturally tamed, and then the fruit of the Way is realized, “indestructible abiding” attained. Therefore the unsurpassed yoga cultivation of the esoteric school is the same as the Chan school, and the Chan school likewise tells you to cultivate without cultivating. Hence the mind-ground method is extremely important.

“When the function is brought to its utmost, though the deluded thoughts of joy, sorrow, and doubt appear the same as those of ordinary beings, one does not, like them, hold the reality of their formation and destruction, and so accumulate the various karmas and turn with the power of desire.”

To bring the function to its utmost is to bring such illuminating practice to its extreme. At that time, “though the deluded thoughts of joy, sorrow, and doubt appear the same as those of ordinary beings” — meeting with misfortune one grieves, meeting with good fortune one rejoices, and in doing things one still has doubts (but never doubt of the teacher or the Dharma, never doubt touching the root) — these joys, sorrows, and doubts are all deluded thoughts, the same as the joys, sorrows, and doubts of ordinary beings. “Yet one does not, like them, hold the reality of their formation and destruction”: one does not, like ordinary beings, take the states one likes, grieves over, or doubts as truly existent. Although one too stirs “the deluded thoughts of joy, sorrow, and doubt,” one does not hold them to death: one understands that “all marks are false,” and does not think there is any real thing that forms or any real thing that is destroyed. Ordinary beings take the states of delusive thought as real, and their minds are never at peace, brooding and nursing resentment, scheming day and night. Affliction, affliction! The whole life of an ordinary being is spent in delusive thought and affliction — how bitter it is! This is delusion. Because of delusion they create karma; because of karma they receive retribution — this is to “accumulate the various karmas and turn with the power of desire.” Ordinary beings are not their own masters; they turn with the power of desire. One who truly applies effort in cultivation, who has brought “the function to its utmost,” may also have “the deluded thoughts of joy, sorrow, and doubt,” but they pass in a single turn; one does not turn with the power of desire, does not brood and nurse resentment, does not scheme without cease day and night. That is the difference! Meeting with a sorrowful matter, such a one does not refrain from weeping; meeting with a joyful matter, such a one does not refrain from laughing. But having wept and laughed, it is over; the mind remains level and even. One who has brought “the function to its utmost” is not someone who cannot laugh at what is joyful or weep at what is sad — not a dead man or a block of wood. When the practice has reached that point, joy and laughter, anger and scolding are all Buddhadharma, all the Way!

blocks.text: 4. The Essentials of Cultivating the Great Mudrā, and Several Possible Byways

inline.s: “When a thought arises, first recognize the mark of the deluded thought, and its mark ceases with it, as when meeting an old acquaintance; next, the deluded thought must cease of itself, as a snake’s knot unties itself; lastly, the deluded thought, neither beneficial nor harmful, subsides, as a thief entering an empty room. This is the most essential secret of the method of liberation.”

When a deluded thought arises, at the very beginning of one’s practice one merely recognizes the various marks of the deluded thought, and the mark of the deluded thought immediately vanishes, just as when one meets someone one knew before. But after this acquaintance leaves, a shadow remains in the mind. Though the deluded thought has vanished, the shadow is still there. Next, when the practice is somewhat better than before, the deluded thought must arise and cease of itself, like a snake that has tied itself in a knot and can untie itself — the clinging mind has loosened. When the practice reaches its final stage, “the deluded thought, neither beneficial nor harmful, subsides”: it is not that the arising of the deluded thought brings harm, nor that its ceasing brings benefit; rather, neither beneficial nor harmful, it naturally subsides. However much deluded thoughts arise, I know they are the true mind’s wondrous function, and so I do not abide, and they naturally cease; I no longer discriminate among deluded thoughts. Some practitioners like to discriminate: Oh! My deluded thoughts no longer arise — how good, my practice has advanced! Alas! Deluded thoughts have arisen again — harmful, harmful, I have fallen back. In fact deluded thoughts have no self-nature and are neither good nor bad; if only we practice earnestly, in the end no mind of “beneficial or harmful” discrimination will arise, and deluded thoughts will subside as they arise. “As a thief entering an empty room” — like a thief entering an empty room, there is nothing to steal. “This is the most essential secret of the method of liberation” — this is the most important and most wondrous method of liberating deluded thoughts.

Since this is “the most essential secret of the method of liberation,” let us go through these three levels of practice once more. When a deluded thought arises, first recognize it and do not run after it, and the deluded thought ceases with that. But at first the power of recognizing deluded thoughts is not sufficient; though the deluded thought has ceased, its shadow is not absent from our minds — it is still there. It is like meeting an old acquaintance: though he has gone, our minds churn — this man unseen for many years, how he was in the past, how he is now. The person has left, but the shadow remains. Though the deluded thought has ceased, its shadow still lingers. This is because the power is not yet full!

Next, one recognizes deluded thoughts further and knows that they must cease of themselves; the power is fuller than before. But the illusory mark of the deluded thought is still there, and it remains for a while before ceasing, like “a snake’s knot untying itself.” A snake does not tie itself in knots; if you tie one for it, after a time it will untie it. When the practice has reached this point, when “the old acquaintance” leaves, the mind no longer churns: compared with before, one has advanced another step.

Still further, one recognizes that deluded thoughts are neither beneficial nor harmful, that their arising and ceasing have nothing to do with me. For the true mind does not move or shake: my true mind is not diminished by a fraction when deluded thoughts arise, nor increased by a fraction when they cease; the true mind neither increases nor decreases. Therefore deluded thoughts are neither beneficial nor harmful — let them arise and cease as they will. To recognize this is the most important thing; to accomplish it is best and most wondrous. If, after a deluded thought has arisen, we still turn it over in the mind, still cannot let it go, still must scheme about it again — that is because the power is not yet full. Many people are like this: they dream at night and on waking must think it over again, what the dream was like, and must tell others about it. If we could accomplish this: knowing it was a dream, paying it no attention, leaving not a shadow in the mind — then we would have power. Meeting an old acquaintance, a snake’s knot untying itself, a thief entering an empty room — these are the different levels of our view of deluded thoughts and of the power to dissolve them. On which level you can dissolve deluded thoughts, you must investigate for yourself.
“Knowing cultivation but not understanding liberation is the same as the heaven-dwellers of dhyāna.”

To know cultivation, to know not to run after deluded thoughts, but not to know that “all deluded thoughts are the wondrous function arising within the self-nature’s all-penetrating state” — this is called “knowing cultivation but not understanding liberation.” To know only the cultivation of the Way, not what the true mind is, not to recognize the true mind — that is “the same as the heaven-dwellers of dhyāna.” However diligently you practice, even to the extreme, with deep concentration, if you do not recognize the true mind, you will be born only in the first, second, third, or fourth dhyāna heaven — still not beyond the form realm. To say nothing of liberation, you will not even reach the formless realm.
“Without the cultivation of such an essential secret of the method of liberation, though the mind can abide firmly in dhyāna, one still falls into the dhyāna of the higher realms.”

To be without the cultivation of such an essential secret of the method of liberation is to “know cultivation but not understand liberation.” “Though the mind can abide firmly in dhyāna” means the mind can be unmoving, entering deep concentration, remaining unmoved for one year, two years, three years, even for one kalpa, two kalpas, or a hundred million kalpas. “One still falls into the dhyāna of the higher realms”: one falls only into the dhyāna of the four dhyāna heavens or the four formless heavens. This is still the dhyāna of the form realm and the formless realm, still within the three realms, and not liberation. Without recognizing the true mind, one cannot leave the three realms, and one is the same as the non-Buddhists. Why can non-Buddhists not leave the three realms? Because they do not know what the true mind is. Non-Buddhists cling to the yang spirit, holding that the yang spirit is real and indestructible. The yang spirit is what Buddhism calls the “mind-born body,” the body produced by the seventh consciousness (the mind-root) — still a false shadow. The Diamond Sutra says: “All marks are false.” Everything with marks is false, and the yang spirit is false too; it does not leave the three realms and is not ultimate. Only by recognizing the true-suchness self-nature and striving to protect it — cultivating in this way — can one accomplish the great Way. We say again and again: everyone must protect the true-suchness dharma-body well! Know it clearly and constantly, be unattached at every moment, guard it closely and continuously, and in time you will naturally realize the great Way and will certainly succeed. To recognize the true mind is like obtaining rice; then use fire to cook it, and it becomes a meal. What is called using fire to cook it is protecting it at every moment, not letting deluded thoughts invade anywhere, not running after deluded thoughts, the mind empty and unattached; then the result is certain Buddhahood. This is extremely important. If one does not cultivate in this way, then even with deep concentration and long hours in dhyāna, one cannot realize the great Way. Many people today admire concentration: Oh, this Dharma master’s practice is excellent — he has been in concentration for a week. Oh no, no! That Dharma master’s practice is even better — three months in concentration. Here we must shout at them: No! That is dead concentration; one absolutely cannot realize the great Way! True dhyāna is to be undeluded by states, to be unattached at all times. To be concentrated while sitting there but not concentrated once off the cushion — is that acceptable? It is not. Therefore, without recognizing the true-suchness dharma-body, blind practice and wild striving absolutely cannot accomplish the Way. You must recognize the true mind and protect it in practice; only then can you accomplish the great Way. This is a principle our students of the Buddhadharma must know, and it is of the utmost importance.
“To be satisfied with merely knowing the arising and abiding of deluded thoughts is no different from the base and wildly deluded.”

Some people, in their practice, come to know where deluded thoughts arise and abide, and are satisfied. They say: “Oh, now I understand. Where deluded thoughts arise and where they abide, I know it all. Where do deluded thoughts arise from? Deluded thoughts arise from states; deluded thoughts are the reflection of states. Where do deluded thoughts abide? They abide on states.” Deluded thoughts do indeed arise from states: without states there would be no deluded thoughts. “Mind is originally unborn; it exists because of states” — this was spoken by the Buddha Viśvabhu. But where do states come from? If one is satisfied with merely knowing the arising and abiding of deluded thoughts, “that is no different from the base and wildly deluded” — no different from the base and wildly deluded. The Buddhadharma is the supreme and wondrous dharma: concentrated without being wild, wise without being deluded. The base and wildly deluded are not the Buddhadharma. “To be satisfied with merely knowing the arising and abiding of deluded thoughts” is the lowest capacity. What use is it to know only the arising and abiding of deluded thoughts? You must recognize the true-suchness dharma-body and apply effort on the dharma-body, illuminating and protecting it at every moment and in every place; only then can you accomplish the Way. To know only the arising and abiding of deluded thoughts and dream of accomplishing the Way is like cooking rice with sand — for millions of kalpas it will never become rice.

“Or one may lean toward emptiness-nature and seek the dharma-body’s seal and correspondence and so on by ratiocination; but when adverse conditions come, what one has cultivated cannot undo the bondage of states, and instead one’s own faults appear.”

One who is satisfied with knowing the arising and abiding of deluded thoughts is of course of inferior capacity, because he is attached to states and takes states to be real. But “leaning toward emptiness-nature” will not do either! To be attached to existence is of course wrong, and to fall into emptiness is wrong too. Why? Because our dharma-body is neither empty nor existent; it is both empty and existent; it is neither empty nor existent — to say it exists is wrong, and to say it is empty is wrong too. “To seek the dharma-body’s seal and correspondence”: a seal is a confirmation, a correspondence is a matching. To seek the dharma-body’s seal and correspondence is to seek to be confirmed by and matched with the dharma-body. If you lean toward emptiness, you do not accord with the dharma-body — how could you be confirmed by and matched with the dharma-body? So one can only call this “ratiocination.” The dharma-body does not fall into ratiocination; once ratiocination enters, one violates the dharma-body. All the various ratiocinations of clinging to emptiness or clinging to existence do not accord with the dharma-body.

But when adverse conditions come, what one has cultivated cannot undo the bondage of states, and instead one’s own faults appear.” When these people who lean toward emptiness meet with evil and adverse conditions, the practice they have done cannot undo the bondage of these states, and they are tied up by them. Their “emptiness” is only ratiocination; when things happen, it cannot be empty at all! Their “emptiness” has an emptiness in it — does that not become “existence”? Long ago there was an elder in Pudong, Shanghai, who said: “You people talk of emptiness, emptiness — how is it there are still mountains, rivers, and the great earth, men and women, young and old?” He understood “emptiness” as “nothing at all,” which is not the same as the emptiness we understand. When we speak of emptiness, we mean the emptiness of marks: do not abide on marks, take the unobtainable as emptiness. “All marks are false” — only do not cling to marks; the marks are still there. Without marks, how could there be wondrous function? If there were no house, how would we shelter from wind and rain? If there were no stool, how would we sit at ease? “Dharmas born of causes and conditions, I say, are emptiness” — having no substance of its own, no self-nature, is emptiness; it is not that there are no marks.

Ratiocinating about “emptiness” is of no use; when states come, one cannot be empty. Our self-nature is neither empty nor existent; it is both empty and existent; existence is emptiness, emptiness is existence. “Existence” in its very substance is unobtainable — that is true emptiness. To cling one-sidedly to emptiness and not recognize the self-nature is to have no power and to be unable to penetrate states. If one recognizes the self-nature, then all states are merely the self-nature’s wondrous function, like reflections in a mirror or waves on water. Recognizing the mirror and knowing the water, one will not be deluded by the reflections and waves, and all states naturally become easy to empty. If one does not recognize the self-nature, they cannot be emptied. First of all we must recognize the true-suchness dharma-body — this is the most important of all. Therefore, clarifying the mind and seeing the nature is fundamental. Whatever school you cultivate, clarifying the mind and seeing the nature is the root; without clarifying the mind and seeing the nature, it will not do.

If one only understands the arising and abiding of deluded thoughts, or leans toward emptiness, and does not recognize the self-nature, then when adverse conditions come, the power of one’s cultivation cannot undo the bondage of states, “and instead one’s own faults appear.” Ordinary beings do not know what true emptiness is; when adverse states appear and they meet obstruction, they are full of doubt and suspicion, and so they slander the Buddhadharma. They say: “This ought to be empty! Why cannot it be empty? It still exists! Then the Buddhadharma is wrong when it speaks of emptiness.” The gods of the four formless heavens are like this: they cultivate to the concentration of emptiness, and when the kalpa of that concentration ends, they emerge from it, see the outer states, and give rise to doubt: “Eh? It is said to be empty — why does it still exist? The Buddha’s teachings deceive people; he is a cheat, a cheat!” They are still clinging to marks; clinging to marks, they create karma; creating karma, they receive retribution. And slandering the Buddhadharma in turn, they fall into hell. This is “instead one’s own faults appear.” Therefore we must recognize the true meaning of the Buddhadharma and know what the Buddha-nature is — this is most important. The Buddha-nature is neither empty nor existent; it is both empty and existent, and it is also empty and also existent. If you cling to emptiness or fall into emptiness and cultivate without recognizing the original nature, your cultivation will not succeed. The result is the creation of evil karma, and instead one’s own faults appear.
“Arising-and-ceasing, self-ceasing, and ceasing-in-concentration: all are deluded thoughts ceasing of themselves; following delusion, one is originally pure.”

If deluded thoughts can arise, they can also cease. There are three forms of ceasing: “arising-and-ceasing, self-ceasing, and ceasing-in-concentration.” Arising-and-ceasing: a later deluded thought arises and does away with the previous deluded thought. Self-ceasing: the deluded thought ceases of itself. Ceasing-in-concentration: one practices and enters concentration, and the deluded thoughts are dissolved.

These several ways of dissolving deluded thoughts differ in speed and in strength. However one dissolves them, it is the deluded thought ceasing of itself; therefore “all are deluded thoughts ceasing of themselves.” In fact, deluded thoughts themselves are false and unobtainable, and there is no such thing as ceasing or not ceasing. Not abiding in them, one regards them as ceased. Once deluded thoughts have ceased, one is “following delusion, originally pure”: following the ceasing of deluded thoughts, one is the originally pure true-suchness dharma-body. The sutra says: “When the mad mind is stilled, that is bodhi.” How does the deluded mind arise? “Mind is originally unborn; it exists because of states” (as the Buddha Viśvabhu plainly said). The deluded mind exists because of states; without outer states there is no deluded mind. But states are as illusory and unobtainable as the mind: “The mind is not mind of itself; it is mind because of states; states are not states of themselves; they are states because of the mind.” Mind and states arise in mutual dependence; apart from one there is no other. Therefore our late master, Elder Xianglu, said: “States too are not there; they are all alike a phantom.” So long as you understand that all outer states are like dreams, illusions, and flowers in the sky, without substantial reality, and do not go seeking them and do not give rise to deluded thoughts, then spirit is calm and wisdom clear, the numinous light shines alone, the true mind is bright and pure, like a mirror reflecting things, neither grasping nor rejecting, neither loving nor hating, utterly distinct yet not a single thought arising, not a single thought arising yet utterly distinct. In that instant you personally realize the true-suchness dharma-body, and there is no need to do any clumsy practice beyond stilling the mind. If you truly recognize the true-suchness dharma-body, deluded thoughts are the true-suchness dharma-body’s wondrous function, and the deluded too is pure. It is like recognizing that the waves themselves are water: not clinging to the marks of the waves, one need not wait for the waves to subside — the waves in their very substance are water. This is the profound meaning of “following delusion, originally pure.”

The central point spoken of here is that we must recognize deluded thoughts and not fear them. Deluded thoughts are the true mind’s wondrous function. So long as one does not run after them, one can cut them off, and following delusion one is originally pure. Following the arising and ceasing of deluded thoughts, one is the fundamentally pure true-suchness dharma-body. The true-suchness dharma-body is itself pure; it does not become impure because of deluded thoughts. So long as one does not run after deluded thoughts, is not swayed by them, attends to the true-suchness dharma-body at every moment, and guards it closely and continuously, in time one will certainly realize the great Way and realize the fruit of Buddhahood.
“This mark of ceasing-and-understanding is the one and only essential of self-liberation’s direct perception.”

Earlier we spoke of following delusion one is originally pure. Where does delusion arise from? Delusion exists following states. If there were no states, there would be no deluded thoughts. Though deluded thoughts arise following deluded states, our true mind is not defiled; it is still pure. We once used the pearl as a metaphor: a pearl wrapped in mud, yet the pearl itself is still pure and luminous — it does not become dark and stained because it is wrapped in mud. Once the mud is removed, the pearl is luminous as before. Therefore one need only recognize the true mind; one need not fear deluded thoughts. To quell the incorrect understanding of deluded thoughts, to untie the knot of fearing deluded thoughts, and thereby to recognize the true mind — this is called the mark of ceasing-and-understanding. “This mark of ceasing-and-understanding is the one and only essential of self-liberation’s direct perception.” Direct perception is to set everything out whole, without adding discrimination, like a mirror reflecting things. Reflecting a round thing, it shows a round mark; reflecting a square thing, it shows a square mark; reflecting ten thousand ounces of gold, the mirror is not pleased; reflecting a heap of dung, the mirror is not angered. This is direct perception. Direct perception manifests following the appearance of objective things, without adding the slightest delusive discrimination. If one discriminates this as good and that as bad, this as long and that as short, this as beautiful and that as ugly, that is inferential knowledge.

In cultivating the path of liberation we turn the eighth consciousness into the great perfect mirror wisdom, which illumines the ten directions, and the myriad phenomena all appear within our true mind, without the slightest love or hate, grasping or rejecting — this is “liberation’s direct perception.” Though we use a mirror as a metaphor, it is not entirely like a mirror. To manifest a form according to objective circumstances is like a mirror. Yet a mirror has no power of discernment, no sentience. We have sentience: we know right and wrong, long and short, gain and loss, only without love and hate, grasping and rejecting. It is exactly as the sutra says: “One is able to discriminate all dharmas’ marks, yet in the primary meaning one does not move.” Though one discriminates, it does not enter the mind — that is direct perception functioning as inferential knowledge. If there were only direct perception, we would become fools and dullards, not even knowing right and wrong, good and bad, long and short — how could that do? Practice must be lively; at every moment we use the direct-perception true mind for the purposes of inferential knowledge. Inferential knowledge is what is called deluded thought. Therefore we must understand the principle the Buddha stated in the Sutra of Perfect Enlightenment: “Toward all deluded minds, likewise do not extinguish them.” Use it when it is needed; being able to use it is wondrous function. This is the profound meaning of “the mark of ceasing-and-understanding.” This mark of ceasing-and-understanding is liberation’s direct perception; it is “the one and only essential” — this is the one thing that matters.

To recognize the true mind is of the greatest importance. Where is the true mind? The true mind is right before every person, shining. Where is the light? I see things, I hear sounds, I smell fragrances and odors, I know all kinds of states — this is the light! Some people single-mindedly extinguish deluded thoughts, but after the deluded thoughts are gone, when the true mind shines clearly before them, they do not recognize the true mind; instead they continue the work of stilling thoughts. Practicing like this, in time they become dead, and do not attain lively wondrous function, because they do not recognize the true mind. We have said above: to still only deluded thoughts and not know the essence is of no use. Where deluded thoughts are stilled, one must recognize the essence — this is the one thing that matters.
“That is, the uncommon essential secret of the supreme dharma-gate of the self-nature’s Great Perfection.”

The Great Perfection has concrete dharmas that can be cultivated, but what is spoken of here is “the self-nature’s Great Perfection.” The self-nature is originally perfect and without lack, originally filling space and pervading the dharma-realm; however vast space is, so vast is it. The worlds of the ten directions and all sentient beings are complete within the self-nature. Whether the Pure Land school, the esoteric school, the Chan school, the Dharma-character school, the Tiantai school, the Huayan school, and so on — none can depart from this wondrous luminous true mind. “Nothing does not flow forth from this dharma-realm; nothing does not return to this dharma-realm.” This dharma-realm is the one true dharma-realm, the wondrous luminous true mind. The Ganges Great Mudrā is the “supreme dharma-gate” that directly enters “the self-nature’s Great Perfection.” Supreme means special; excellent means superior. This is a specially superior dharma, which other dharmas cannot match; it is “uncommon” to other dharmas. Common means shared; uncommon means not the same. This is the dharma of the highest single vehicle in the esoteric school; the other vehicles in the esoteric school do not speak in this way. The highest esoteric dharma and the Chan school breathe through one nostril. The Pure Land school does not speak in this way: it stresses single-minded Buddha-recitation and rebirth in the Western Land of Ultimate Bliss. After reaching the Western Land of Ultimate Bliss, one continues to cultivate in the company of Buddhas and bodhisattvas and realizes the stage of non-retrogression — avaivartika. There are wonders in that, and in the end it too converges in the one true dharma-realm; we will not speak of it at length here. Every dharma-gate has its own wonders and its own opportunities for responding and transforming, and in the end all converge in the one true dharma-realm. But the Ganges Great Mudrā is direct entry, without detours, unlike other methods of cultivation; that is “the uncommon essential secret of the supreme dharma-gate of the self-nature’s Great Perfection.” Yao means the essential point; miao means the wondrous. The uncommon essential secret is the essential point unlike other dharma-gates, the uniquely possessed wonder.
“Possessing this essential secret, whatever affliction or deluded thought arises is manifested as the dharma-body.”

To possess this essential secret is to recognize the true mind’s wondrous function. Once you possess this essential secret, “whatever affliction or deluded thought arises is manifested as the dharma-body.” Whatever affliction it may be — illness, the pain of a broken romance, failure in one’s career, and so on — that is, when afflictions swarm and deluded thoughts seethe, all is manifested as the dharma-body. Because “deluded thoughts and afflictions are all the dharma-body’s original-enlightenment wisdom marks.” Just as without water there are no waves, without the true mind where would afflictions and deluded thoughts come from? When afflictions and deluded thoughts rise up, that is the manifestation of the dharma-body. Everyone must understand that this sentence is extremely important. When afflictions swarm and deluded thoughts seethe, recognize at once that this is the dharma-body’s wondrous function, and the afflictions and deluded thoughts crumble and melt on the spot. Having recognized the dharma-body, one does not run after deluded thoughts; not having recognized the dharma-body, one runs after deluded thoughts, afflictions are endless, and one may even want to kill oneself. Some people today, broken-hearted in love, are so afflicted and miserable that they want to commit suicide, unable to go on living. They do not recognize the dharma-body, do not understand that afflictions and deluded thoughts are all the true mind’s wondrous function!

The Universal Gateway Chapter of the Bodhisattva Avalokiteśvara says: “If there be one who holds the name of the Bodhisattva Avalokiteśvara, though he enter a great fire, the fire cannot burn him, because of the Bodhisattva’s awesome spiritual power; if he be swept away by great waters and calls the name, he straightway reaches a shallow place.” However great the fire of your afflictions and however high the waves of your deluded thoughts, so long as you turn the light around and reflect, and call “Namo Avalokiteśvara Bodhisattva,” oh! This is originally the true mind’s wondrous function! Those afflictions and deluded thoughts are stilled at once — this is the secret, the most important secret. Not a few people have studied Buddhism for many years without knowing this secret; they do not recognize the true mind, do not know where the true mind is. They cannot find it — what then? They go to the Western Land of Ultimate Bliss to look for it, and that is more than ten thousand li away! In fact the true mind is shining right before you. The Great Mudrā is excellent: it tells us directly and plainly what the true mind is. You all have blessings and your opportunities have ripened, and so you are able to hear this great dharma. Having heard this great dharma, do not fail yourselves; protect the true mind at every moment, understand that where deluded thoughts arise is the true mind’s wondrous function, and recognize the true mind from within deluded thoughts. Practicing thus — one year, two years, three or five years — will you not accomplish the Way? You will certainly succeed. Last time I said that my master (the guru Wang Xianglu) said: “In practice it takes no two or three years; a year and a half will succeed. If you do not succeed, come and ask me.” We simply refuse to practice, always running after our habitual tendencies — how can we succeed?
“Deluded thoughts all become wisdom, adverse conditions become helpful companions, afflictions become the Way.”

If one possesses this “uncommon essential secret of the supreme dharma-gate of the self-nature’s Great Perfection,” then “deluded thoughts all become wisdom.” Just when deluded thoughts fly about and afflictions swarm, give a keen turn: Oh! This is the dharma-body’s wondrous function! To be able to turn thus is great wisdom. Facing states, direct perception functioning as inferential knowledge — not clinging to states, not sticking to states, not abiding in states, yet not failing to know beauty and ugliness, right and wrong — this is wisdom. If after discriminating one must grasp and reject, abiding in states and sticking in the mind, running after states, miserable to death, bound fast — that is deluded thought. In fact deluded thought is wisdom; the key lies in whether you know it or not. Therefore “toward all deluded minds, likewise do not extinguish them.” If the true-suchness dharma-body is master, deluded thoughts become servants, hired hands. The master directs the servants to do work, and that is “the wisdom of accomplished action.” When the true mind is master, the first five consciousnesses (eye, ear, nose, tongue, and body) are transformed into the wisdom of accomplished action. The true mind directs them: show me what this thing is; let me hear what sound this is; let me smell whether this is fragrant or foul; let me taste whether this is sour or sweet… Seeing, hearing, sensing, and knowing all become the true mind’s wondrous function — deluded thoughts all become wisdom.

Adverse conditions become helpful companions.” Everyone likes the Western Land of Ultimate Bliss; in the Western Land of Ultimate Bliss everything is a favorable condition, nothing is displeasing. The ground is gold, there are seven-jeweled ponds and the water of eight meritorious qualities, water-birds and trees, the sound of wind and the speech of birds — all proclaim the Dharma-sound; all is good, and there are no enemies or adversaries. Unlike this evil world of the five turbidities, where afflictions and enemies are beyond counting. For example, in work there are many displeasing things: this person steps on your foot, that person kicks your leg; at home too there is much that goes against your heart — you think one way and she insists on another, you do one thing and she insists on another — the household is full of quarrels and disputes! But you must understand that these adverse conditions are companions who help you accomplish the Way; they make you alert, so that you do not abide in states. When you understand that these adverse conditions are suffering, you give rise to the mind of renunciation: Alas! This world is so bitter — quickly escape the suffering! How does one escape suffering? Recognize the true mind and do not run after states. Otherwise you stick to this world and cannot bear to leave, thinking this world truly agreeable and truly comfortable, and then you do not study Buddhism or cultivate the Dharma, and you cannot accomplish the Way. I once met an overseas Chinese in France; he had a great deal of money, and the warehouse of his home was connected to a railway, so that a train could drive right in. He also believed in the Buddhadharma and did many good deeds; whenever he returned to China to visit relatives he would always go to a temple to give alms. I said to him: “You believe in the Buddhadharma and are willing to give alms; it would be even better if you cultivated the Buddhadharma yourself. Doing good deeds and giving alms alone is cultivating merit and blessings; it cannot accomplish the Way. You must also cultivate wisdom; only by cultivating both blessings and wisdom can you accomplish the Way. So you still need to study and cultivate the Buddhadharma.” He said: “No, no, I am too comfortable and too happy; I have no need to endure hardship in cultivation.” He was sunk in blessings and rewards, satisfied with the status quo, unwilling to cultivate. If people are like this, how much more so the gods?

If you meet all kinds of adverse conditions, eat bitterness to the full, and feel it keenly as suffering, then you should arouse the great mind to escape suffering. To escape suffering, what should you do? Quickly study and cultivate the Buddhadharma — and so it is said that “adverse conditions become helpful companions.” Adverse conditions help you train amid states: do they show whether your mind still abides in states or not? If your mind is truly empty, then favorable and adverse are all the same, and it makes no difference whether you run after things or not. Among the ten great vows of Samantabhadra Bodhisattva there is the vow to “constantly accord with sentient beings.” To constantly accord with sentient beings is to always follow along with them. You like to eat spicy food — fine! I will eat spicy food with you; you like sweet food — fine! I will eat sweet food with you; you want to play ball — fine! I will play ball with you; you want to dance — fine! I will dance with you; you want to believe in Christianity — fine! I will believe in Christianity along with you. Everything is all right. Why? To train the true mind! I am empty and have nothing to attain; everything is the true mind’s wondrous function. Running along with you is also wondrous function, in order to gather you in; this is called “the gathering of fellow-workers.” A bodhisattva practices the four means of gathering, and among them is “the gathering of fellow-workers.” Not a few cultivators of the Way do not wish to be born in the Western Pure Land — why? Because the Western Land of Ultimate Bliss is a realm of favorable conditions, and the time needed to accomplish the Way there is very long. One day in the Western Land of Ultimate Bliss equals one great kalpa here. How many days is a great kalpa? So many that it is hard to reckon. A great kalpa has four intermediate kalpas; an intermediate kalpa has twenty small kalpas. How long is each small kalpa? Suppose a human lifespan is eighty-four thousand years; every hundred years it decreases by one year, until the lifespan is ten years, and then every hundred years it increases by one year again, until it is eighty-four thousand years once more. This one increase and one decrease is the length of a small kalpa. Eighty such small kalpas make one great kalpa. How many days is that? One day in the Western Land of Ultimate Bliss equals so long a time here. Add to that the fact that over there all is favorable conditions, everything goes as your mind wishes: whatever kind of house you want, you have such a house; whatever clothes you want, you have them; whatever you want to use, you have it. So the habitual tendencies are not easily exhausted, and the time needed to accomplish the Way is long. Therefore many bodhisattvas who have aroused the great mind say: You go to the Western Land of Ultimate Bliss; I will train the true mind here in the Saha world, training amid adverse conditions. This is the spirit of a bodhisattva of the great mind, rare and precious! “A true man has of himself a soaring ambition; he does not journey to the Brahmā heavens or the Pure Land.” Not going to the great Brahmā heavens or the Pure Land — that is the bearing of a true man. If you truly have the bearing of a true man, you must be able to withstand training. If you cannot withstand training and are seized by the demon king, becoming a son or grandson of the demon, then you are finished. If you cannot withstand the training, then you had better go to the Western Land of Ultimate Bliss, which is far more stable than here. Therefore the Dharma has no fixed dharma; it depends on each person’s spirit and each person’s capacity. Nothing is fixed and unchangeable. In our present cultivation and practice, when we meet adverse circumstances we must not lose heart: these are helpful companions that help us accomplish the Way.

I have a Dharma brother whose wife believes in Christianity and dragged him to a Christian church. He said: “Fine, fine, I will go with you.” After hearing the pastor’s sermon, he said to her: “I went with you to hear the pastor preach; now you come with me to the temple and hear a great good teacher of Buddhism expound the Buddhadharma.” She said: “I will not go, I will not go — that is the demon king. You are not allowed to go either. Let us go home.” So he went home with her. On the face of it this is an adverse condition, but he was not afraid of it. You cannot grind me down; I accord with you, my mind is empty, and I am perfectly at ease and free. So their relationship as husband and wife was very good. She asked: “Do you say I am the demon king?” He answered: “No, I say you are very good; you are a great bodhisattva.” She said: “I am not a great bodhisattva; I am God, the Lord.” He answered at once: “Fine, fine! You are God, the Lord.” All of these are helpful companions, training your mind to be empty! A poem puts it well: “Empty, empty, empty — in emptiness success is won. If the root is firmly planted, what matter snow and wind?” When the root is firm, you do not fear great snow or wild wind; when all adverse states come, you do not fear them, for you must know they are our companions on the Way! Adverse conditions are good things too; do not fear them.

Afflictions become the Way.” Speaking of the Way, some say: White Maiden had only five hundred years of the Way; Fahai had a thousand years of the Way. In fact those are all myths; there never was any White Maiden. If we can make use of afflictions, awakening within affliction — this is my true mind’s wondrous function! — then affliction helps you accomplish the Way, and affliction becomes the Way. The greater the affliction, the higher the Way. If you can withstand the training of affliction until the mind is empty, your power is great, and you can be forged and grow within the blazing fire of affliction — this is “the lotus born in fire is never destroyed.” This is tremendous practice. A lotus in water cannot withstand fire; roast it once and it is finished. Only the lotus born in fire has strong vitality.
“Not abandoning transmigration, yet abiding in purity.”

Transmigration means the six paths of transmigration: gods, humans, asuras, hell-beings, hungry ghosts, and animals. Truly to understand birth and death thoroughly need not mean leaving the six paths of transmigration. Why? Because if you merely abide in a pure land outside the three realms — outside the desire realm, the form realm, and the formless realm — then you are only a Hīnayāna arhat. If you would become a Buddha, you must have the conduct of a bodhisattva of the great mind, delivering beings within the six paths, not abandoning transmigration. Here is a case: after a certain Chan master passed into nirvāṇa, someone asked his disciple: “Into what pure land was your master born? The Western Land of Ultimate Bliss, or the Eastern Pure Lapis Lazuli World, or the Inner Court of Tuṣita?” He answered: “My master went neither east nor west.” Asked, “If he went neither east nor west, where did he go?” he answered: “He is an ox in the eastern house and a horse in the western house.” The questioner said: “You are cursing your master!” The answerer laughed: “Ha ha, blue sky, blue sky! An injustice, an injustice!” His meaning was: I am praising my master, and you say I am cursing him — what an injustice! My master’s Way was deep and he had assurance, and so he dared to be “an ox in the eastern house and a horse in the western house,” to walk among other kinds of beings, “not abandoning transmigration, yet abiding in purity.” Do you have that assurance? This is my praise, and you do not understand it. Therefore this “blue sky, blue sky” has a great wonder in it.

Chan Master Zhaozhou was known as “the Old Buddha of Zhaozhou.” When he spoke it was wondrous indeed — soft as a ball of cotton, yet you dare not squeeze it. Why? Because there is a needle hidden in the cotton; squeeze it and it pricks your hand. Once he wanted to go to Mount Tiantai to see Amitābha Buddha. Who was Amitābha Buddha? Chan Master Fenggan was an emanation of Amitābha Buddha. Under Chan Master Fenggan were Hanshan and Shide, emanations of Mañjuśrī Bodhisattva and Samantabhadra Bodhisattva. Chan Master Zhaozhou came to Mount Tiantai just after rain, and the ground was clearly covered with many ox-hoof prints. He saw a boy riding on an ox’s back playing a flute; this boy was Hanshan. The boy asked Zhaozhou: “Does the senior abide in the ox or not?” “Senior” is a respectful title for a monk. He asked Chan Master Zhaozhou: Do you still recognize the ox? If he had answered “I recognize it,” he would have fallen into the trap, proving that he had not gone beyond the ordinary being’s realm of clinging to states and sticking in the mind. Another Chan master, Danxia Tianran, once asked a visiting monk: “Where do you come from?” The monk said: “From down the mountain.” Danxia said: “Have you eaten or not?” The monk said: “I have eaten.” Danxia said: “Does the one who brought you food to eat have eyes or not?” Has the one who gave you food grown eyes? The meaning is that he mistook his man, making an offering to a worldly fellow who clings to states and sticks in the mind. Chan Master Zhaozhou was a master of the great brush; he would not fall into this trap. Hanshan asked: “Does the senior recognize the ox or not?” Zhaozhou answered: “I do not recognize it.” This is just like Bodhidharma’s answer to Emperor Wu of Liang. Emperor Wu asked: “Who is it that stands before me?” Bodhidharma said: “I do not recognize it.” Did Bodhidharma not even recognize himself? Did Chan Master Zhaozhou not even recognize an ox? That is not the meaning! To fix one’s eyes on recognizing or not recognizing is wrong in either case. Bodhidharma’s answer “I do not recognize it” was aimed at the “who” in the question; Chan Master Zhaozhou’s answer “I do not recognize it” was aimed at the “ox” in the question. The two answers come from the same track: both sweep away all stickiness and transcend all subject-object opposition, not abiding on “who,” not abiding on “ox,” and set out whole the bare, clean, numinous true mind. When Hanshan heard Chan Master Zhaozhou answer “I do not recognize it,” he pointed at the ox-hoof prints and said: “These are five hundred arhats roaming the mountain.” Zhaozhou asked: “Since they are arhats, why have they become oxen?” Hanshan said: “Blue sky, blue sky!” What does this mean? It means: your discriminating mind is blazing. All sentient beings are Buddhas, all possess the Tathāgata’s wisdom and virtue marks, and still you discriminate arhats and oxen from hoof prints! “Blue sky, blue sky!” covered Chan Master Zhaozhou. But Zhaozhou was after all a master of the great brush, skilled at turning where there is no place to turn, like taiji push-hands: four ounces deflect a thousand catties. So he laughed aloud. Hanshan asked: “What are you doing?” What are you laughing at? Zhaozhou said: “Blue sky, blue sky!” The meaning is: you ask “what are you doing?” — still there is a thing there! Hanshan praised him: “This one here truly has the manner of a great man.” You possess the strategy of a true man, the bearing of one who is liberated.

The Chan school tells us to see the nature at every moment, to see the nature in all functions, not to run after states. Chan Master Yongjia said: “Walking is Chan, sitting is Chan; speaking or silent, moving or still, the essence is at peace.” Chan school, Chan school — everywhere is Chan, at every moment the school; hence it is said: “Every day is a good day.” Therefore, “not abandoning transmigration, yet abiding in purity.” When the essence is pure, every place is a place of practice; is there still a mark of transmigration to be got at?
“Liberated from the entanglements of defilement and purity, one cultivates and corrects without effort, spontaneously.”

To discriminate endlessly between defilement and purity is to be entangled and bound by the concepts of defilement and purity. To be liberated from such entanglement is “liberated from the entanglements of defilement and purity.” The Diamond Sutra says: “One should give rise to the mind that abides in nothing.” Ying means to accord with; abiding in nothing means not sticking: according with all conditions without sticking, giving rise to the numinous, wondrous, unattached mind — this is “cultivating and correcting without effort.” Bodhisattvas before the eighth ground all cultivate and correct with effort. For example, we teach everyone to attend to the original at every moment; attending is cultivation and correction with effort. But if you do not attend, it will not do — habitual tendencies are heavy! Once you forget, you abide in marks and states again, and run after deluded thoughts again. Therefore one must attend and illuminate at every moment; this is the method of transforming from effort to effortlessness. Only bodhisattvas from the eighth ground upward can “cultivate and correct without effort, spontaneously.” To cultivate and correct means not to be scattered, to have right mindfulness clear and bright at every moment, utterly distinct, awake and still, still and awake. Effortless means that even the mind of illumination is gone — this is “cultivating and correcting without effort.” Everyone, take note: this is not asking you to do it right now, but to go from effort to effortlessness. When cultivating and correcting with effort, do not think that such cultivation is enough, that you have cultivated well. We must advance, advance, and advance further: the eighth, ninth, and tenth grounds do not count; the two enlightenments of equal and wondrous do not count either; only ultimate enlightenment — perfect Buddhahood — is the end. So you must strive in practice; only when practice reaches its limit can one be spontaneous. We must begin from “cultivating and correcting with effort” — otherwise how could one reach the stage of “cultivating and correcting without effort”? That requires recognizing the true mind where deluded thoughts are stilled, and protecting it at every moment. This is the most important point.
“Without this power of the method of liberation, though one has the highest view and the profoundest cultivation, it is of no benefit to the mind.”

The method of liberation” is to recognize the dharma-body. If one only knows to practice to death, or explains the principle very well, but does not recognize the dharma-body, then one is “without this power of the method of liberation.” Without this power of the Way, “though one has the highest view and the profoundest cultivation, it is of no benefit to the mind.” The highest view means understanding many principles and explaining them well. The profoundest cultivation means sitting well and entering deep concentration. Without recognizing the dharma-body, these alone will not do. Chan Master Xiangyan was originally a disciple of Chan Master Baizhang. He was very clever and thoroughly versed in the sutras, treatises, and Chan sayings; ask him one thing and he answered ten. But he lacked the power of the method of liberation and had not recognized the dharma-body. After Chan Master Baizhang passed into nirvāṇa, Xiangyan went to consult his senior Dharma brother, Chan Master Weishan. When Chan Master Weishan saw Xiangyan coming, he said to him: “I hear that when you were with our late master Baizhang, ask you one thing and you answered ten, ask you ten and you answered a hundred. This is your cleverness and sharpness, your intellectual understanding and conceptual thinking — the root of birth and death. Before your parents were born, try and say a word!” Xiangyan was stumped and had no answer. He searched the scriptures, he searched the writings he had read, and could not find a single answering phrase. He sighed for himself: “A painted cake cannot fill the belly,” and repeatedly begged Chan Master Weishan to explain it for him. Weishan said: “If I explained it to you, you would curse me later. What I say is mine, and in the end has nothing to do with you.”

Therefore, if one does not possess the power of the Way of liberation, it is of no practical benefit to the cultivation of mind. Chan Master Xiangyan then burned all the writings he usually read, and said in anger: “In this life I will not study the Buddhadharma. I will be a long-walking gruel-and-rice monk, and spare the toil of mind.” Then he wept farewell to Chan Master Weishan and went to dwell in an abandoned old temple (a relic of National Master Zhong of Nanyang), plowing and eating his own food. He burned his writings and did not study the Buddhadharma, sweeping away “the highest view”; long-walking for gruel and rice, sparing the toil of mind, he set aside “the profoundest cultivation.” But the huatou “before your parents were born” he never forgot, at any time or place. The Chan school’s method of investigating the huatou was advocated with great force by Chan Master Dahui Zonggao of the Song dynasty and swept through the Chan groves. Chan Master Xiangyan was a man of the Tang dynasty, when the Chan school mostly used direct pointing, and investigating the huatou was not widely practiced. Chan Master Xiangyan may be said to have opened the way for “investigating the huatou.” He investigated while walking, while sitting, while plowing in the fields — exactly as it is said: “Walking, standing, sitting, and lying down, never apart from this.” He not only cast aside worldly fame and profit and left home to study the Way, but also swept away all concepts of “enlightenment” and “accomplishing the Way,” and settled his mind in one place. Practicing thus for a long time, good news was about to come. One day, clearing wasteland and planting fields, he drove his hoe through the soil and struck a piece of tile; he picked it up and threw it, and it happened to hit a bamboo at the edge of the field. With a “crack,” it shook awake the great dream of birth and death, and in an instant the original was opened. Oh! So that is how it is. In the Chan school this is called “breaking through the huatou” — breaking through and penetrating the huatou one has been investigating. So what was the face before your parents were born? Chan Master Xiangyan did not reveal it. Fortunately he did not reveal it; otherwise “before your parents were born” could not afterward have been used as a huatou to investigate. With a ready-made answer, the doubt-sensation could not be raised.

In the Song dynasty, because of Chan Master Dahui’s advocacy, huatou investigation flourished. There was a monk who also investigated the huatou “before your parents were born.” He was not like Chan Master Xiangyan, who burned his writings and did not study the Buddhadharma and long-walked for gruel and rice, sparing the toil of mind; he did not sweep away the highest view and the profoundest cultivation completely, so he could not spare the toil of mind, and he investigated the huatou too urgently. In time he went mad, muttering to himself, sleeping in the streets and alleys; yet “the original face before my parents were born” he never forgot at any time or place. One day he came upon two brothers fighting, and their uncle stepped forward to stop them. The uncle said: “When your father was alive, he was a man with a face…” A “face” means prestige, standing. As soon as the monk heard “with a face,” he stupidly squeezed into the crowd of onlookers, wanting to find this face. The uncle criticized his two nephews: “And you two are fighting — what does that look like? So faceless!” As soon as the monk heard “faceless,” suddenly empty space shattered and the great earth sank away, true suchness appeared clearly before him, he broke through the huatou and was enlightened. From then on he was neither mad nor foolish, and went off free and at ease. “Faceless” is the markless true mark, it is the self-nature! To know only the theory of marklessness without seeing the self-nature is to have no ground to stand on; though you speak flowers raining from heaven and golden lotuses springing from the earth, it is of no use. It must be brought home in the depths of the mind-ground and the self-nature clearly seen; only then can one penetrate all states.

After Chan Master Xiangyan broke through the huatou and awakened to the Way, he bathed, burned incense, and bowed from afar toward Weishan, saying: “The Master is greatly compassionate; his kindness exceeds that of my parents. Had he explained it for me then, how would there be today’s matter!” Then he had a verse: “One blow, and what I knew was forgotten; no longer relying on cultivation. In movement and countenance I raise the ancient road; I do not fall into the quiet trap. Everywhere without trace or track, beyond sound and form the bearing. All the adepts of the Way in every quarter say this is the highest of the highest.” This verse reached Weishan, and Chan Master Weishan said to his eminent disciple Chan Master Yangshan: “This one has penetrated.” But Yangshan said: “This is the mind’s mechanism and consciousness, composed by writing. Wait until I have examined him in person.” He wanted to test Xiangyan himself. When Yangshan met Xiangyan, he said: “The Master praises my junior brother for uncovering the great matter; try and say it for me.” Xiangyan brought out the former verse; Yangshan said: “This was made by memory of former habits. If you have a true awakening, say something else.” Xiangyan spoke another verse: “Last year’s poverty was not yet poverty; this year’s poverty is poverty indeed. Last year’s poverty still had ground to stand a cone on; this year’s poverty has not even a cone.” Yangshan said: “The Tathāgata Chan I grant that you, junior brother, understand; the patriarchs’ Chan you have not even dreamed of.” Chan Master Xiangyan made yet another verse: “I have a mechanism: I glance and look at him.
