If people do not understand, call in the novice.” When Yangshan heard it he was overjoyed and reported to Weishan: “Let us rejoice that junior brother Xian understands the patriarchs’ Chan.” Chan Master Xiangyan’s Dharma name was Zhixian, and so Yangshan called him “junior brother Xian.” He had originally studied Chan under Chan Master Baizhang, but later, spurred on by Chan Master Weishan, he awakened and became a disciple of Chan Master Weishan. We cannot draw this out too far here; we will not explain this case further, but leave it for you to penetrate yourselves.

Do not suppose that because so many people are here listening to the lecture, their feet are firmly planted. If they lack “the power of the Way of liberation,” their footing may not be steady. As soon as someone says, how good my dharma is, how wondrous, how lofty, they slide right over, wanting to learn “the highest view.” As soon as someone says, how powerful my dharma is, what great superknowledges it can produce, they immediately run after it, wanting to learn “the profoundest cultivation.” They do not understand that the true mind is the root! “Without this power of the method of liberation, though one has the highest view and the profoundest cultivation, it is of no benefit to the mind.” Your theories cannot stand against birth and death; your superknowledges do not count as liberation. Without recognizing the root, there is no use. Without attaining the superknowledge of the extinction of defilements, even if one develops the five superknowledges, they are demonic superknowledges. Not only can they not liberate you, there is the danger of falling into demonic ways. Because “without the power of the Way of liberation… it is of no benefit to the mind”!
“If the power of affliction has not receded, it is not the true Way.”

Why is “the power of the Way of liberation” so important? Because without this power of the Way one does not recognize the markless true mind, and that is “if the power of affliction has not receded, it is not the true Way.” If the power of affliction in your mind has not receded and you are always amid affliction, this is not the true great Way of liberation. In studying Buddhism we must recognize the root and thereby obtain this “power of the Way of liberation”; this is “the true Way,” and we must not follow heretical demons and outsiders. Following heretical demons and outsiders, in the future you will become a son or grandson of the demon, and will not become a Buddha!

“If one attains this essential secret of self-arising and self-ceasing, though one has no reliance whatsoever on the highest view’s method of holding or the profoundest cultivation’s method, one’s own nature will certainly be liberated from the entanglements of the two clingings.”

We have recognized that deluded thoughts are fundamentally unobtainable, so there is no need to bother with them or suppress them; let them arise and cease of themselves. At the moment when “arising and ceasing vanish with it,” “following delusion one is originally pure”; turn the light for a glance, seize it in one grab, and thereby recognize the true mind — then one has “this essential secret of self-arising and self-ceasing.” When we sit in meditation and a thought comes, do not pay it any attention; just hold the mantra and let the thought arise and cease of itself. If you want to suppress it and mutter in your mind, “do not arise, do not arise,” your chest will feel tight, and you will be tense, miserable, and very uncomfortable. Many people’s tight chests are just this: they are too tense. So long as you do not run after the thoughts and let them arise and cease of themselves, you will be relaxed and refreshed, and in time you will become concentrated. As your mantra-recitation deepens, you gradually enter concentration, and from concentration wisdom opens. It is so when sitting in meditation, and so at ordinary times. It is like the crossroads of Nanjing Road and Xizang Road (busy places in Shanghai): people come and go, carriages come and go. Their coming has nothing to do with you; if you do not pull at them, they pass by. When a thought arises, let it arise; it arises and ceases of itself, does not last long, and naturally ceases. But if a thought comes and you do not know it, then you are lost. To be plainly running after deluded thoughts without knowing it, plainly seeking and abiding — how is that cultivation? Therefore, to see the thought and not run after it, to let it arise and cease of itself — this is extremely important. “If one attains this essential secret of self-arising and self-ceasing, though one has no reliance whatsoever on the highest view’s method of holding or the profoundest cultivation’s method, one’s own nature will certainly be liberated from the entanglements of the two clingings.”

The highest view’s method of holding” is the “highest view” spoken of in the previous sentence. “The profoundest cultivation’s method of reliance” is “the profoundest cultivation.” To have a “highest view” to hold and a “profoundest cultivation” to rely on — neither is reliable. “The power of the Way of liberation,” that is, “this essential secret of self-arising and self-ceasing,” is what matters most. The previous sentence says that if one does not attain the essential secret, then even with a high view and deep cultivation one is not liberated. This sentence says that if one attains this essential secret, even without high view and deep cultivation one can still be liberated. These two sentences stress the importance of “the power of the Way of liberation” from the reverse and the positive side. In fact, to attain this essential secret is precisely what deserves to be called the highest view, and to possess this power of the Way is precisely the profoundest cultivation. The loftiness and profundity of view and cultivation spoken of earlier are marked and relative loftiness and profundity; to attain this essential secret and possess this power of the Way is transcendent, mark-free, absolute loftiness and profundity.

One’s own nature will certainly be liberated from the entanglements of the two clingings.” “The two clingings” means clinging to the two extremes, and there are many ways of speaking of it. Clinging to good and clinging to bad; clinging to existence and clinging to nonexistence; clinging to right and clinging to wrong; clinging to emptiness and clinging to existence; and also the clinging to a self in persons and the clinging to a self in dharmas. There are many two-clingings! All lean toward the two extremes. “The clinging to a self in persons” is to take this body or this thought as “I.” This is me; with me as master, you must all not resist, you must all comply with me, carry out my opinions, obey my will — pride and arrogance all come. The Two Vehicles, that is, arhats and pratyekabuddhas, have already eliminated “the clinging to a self in persons,” but still have “the clinging to a self in dharmas” — that there are dharmas to cultivate and a Way to accomplish. The Mahāyāna emptiness school speaks of “emptiness”; its view is very lofty and its theories very fine. But one must not cling; to cling is to “cling to emptiness.” The Mahāyāna existence school, such as the Dharma-character school, speaks of “existence”; its view is also very lofty and its theories also very fine. But one must not cling either; to cling is to “cling to existence.” People have been clinging for many lives and kalpas and are long accustomed to it, deeply bound and entangled by “the two clingings,” that is, “the entanglements of the two clingings.” They tie us up so that we are not liberated. But if you attain “this essential secret of self-arising and self-ceasing” and possess “the power of the Way of liberation,” they cannot tie you for long, and you will certainly be liberated from “the entanglements of the two clingings.”
“As when one has reached the Golden Continent, seeking another stone is utterly unobtainable.”

The Golden Continent is a place that is pure gold. Is there such a place? Not only is there — there are places even better. The Western Land of Ultimate Bliss is better than the Golden Continent. In the Western Land of Ultimate Bliss it is impossible to find a stone. The towers, terraces, halls, and pavilions are not made of stone or brick either; they are made of the seven treasures, exceedingly solid, filled with radiance. If you reach the “Golden Continent” — a place that is pure gold — you fundamentally cannot find any stone that is not gold: “seeking another stone is utterly unobtainable.” This is a metaphor: if we attain the essential secret of arising and ceasing and possess the power of the Way of liberation, it is like reaching the Golden Continent, where there is nothing but gold — a metaphor that there is nothing but liberation, so that one can only attain liberation and nothing else, and will certainly accomplish the Way.
“Whatever moving or still delusive thoughts arise are all only the ready-made true state of concentration.”

This sentence means: whatever delusive thoughts arise, whether moving delusive thoughts or still delusive thoughts, they can only be the ready-made true state of concentration; they are no longer delusive thoughts at all. Just as “when one has reached the Golden Continent, seeking another stone is utterly unobtainable,” so when one has arrived here, there is only the true state of concentration, and no delusive thought can be found. Why can delusive thoughts turn into the true state of concentration? Because one has attained the essential secret of arising and ceasing and possesses the power of the Way of liberation.

You may ask: delusive thoughts are all moving; are there still delusive thoughts? Yes. Seeking stillness is also a delusive thought: to single-mindedly pursue entering concentration, to insist on remaining in concentration for several kalpas, to abide in concentration, to have a state of concentration to attain — this is the still delusive thought. So we say that when sitting in meditation one should not have the yearning to enter concentration. To seek concentration the moment one sits down is precisely the “still delusive thought.” Once the delusive thought arises, the whole sitting is spoiled. One should enter in accordance with conditions, not caring whether one is concentrated or not, always reciting the mantra without pause, one phrase following another, and then one naturally enters concentration. Again, to know clearly that the environment does not allow it and the conditions are not present, yet insist on thinking of a secluded place to cultivate — this too is a “still delusive thought.” “Moving delusive thoughts” are even more numerous: wanting this and that is all moving delusive thought.

Though moving and still delusive thoughts are many, all of them are the ready-made true state of concentration. Thoughts arise and thoughts cease — pay them no attention; recognize the true mind at every moment, recognize the original face, do not run after delusive thoughts, and you will of course be liberated, and of course be in a state of concentration. We have said it is not that sitting there motionless to death is concentration; rather, to be undeluded by states, so that whatever state appears the mind does not waver — this is the great concentration that is neither entering nor emerging. For example, a maiden of sixteen, a girl in the bloom of youth — what is she? A white skeleton, a stinking husk, foul beyond words; what is there to look at? Why does your mind move when you see her? Why do you run after her? Plainly it is the mind of lust at work. “The body of a maiden of sixteen is soft as butter; a sword at her waist beheads the common man. Though no head is seen to fall, in secret the marrow is dried to dust.” Lust is the root of birth and death! Everyone, if lust is not cut off, the Western Land of Ultimate Bliss cannot be reached. Someone says: Between husband and wife, is it not proper lust? Ha ha! Proper lust between husband and wife merely follows your habits; it is spoken of as an expedient. Knowing that the lustful mind of husband and wife cannot be cut off at once, one speaks of proper lust between husband and wife, with the intent that one must not commit sexual misconduct. Speaking ultimately, proper lust must be cut off too! Why? To be born in the Western Land of Ultimate Bliss one must cut off the mind of lust. If lust is not cut off, one is not pure and does not accord with the Pure Land — how could one be born in the Pure Land? The mind of lust is the worst: even if you have developed superknowledges, once the mind of lust comes, the superknowledges are gone. After Chan Master Yunmen had been a king for three lifetimes, his superknowledges were utterly gone. In a former life he was a human king with three palaces and six courts and seventy-two consorts — too many women — and his superknowledges were entirely lost. In India there was a great arhat whose flesh body could fly. A king invited this arhat to his palace for offerings, and the arhat flew straight into the palace. The king, revering the great arhat, had the queen come out to offer wine. The queen was very beautiful, and when the arhat saw her his mind moved a little. In that instant the superknowledges were gone, and he could not fly back. There are many such examples; therefore the mind of lust must not be stirred!
“Again seeking one who is deluded about the self-nature — utterly unobtainable.”

After recognizing the self-nature, one guards it closely and continuously at every moment and in every place, and in time one accomplishes the Way. Then if one turns back to seek the ignorance and delusive thought that are deluded about the self-nature, one can never find them again — “again seeking one who is deluded about the self-nature — utterly unobtainable.” Someone asks: I recognize the Buddha-nature and am no longer deluded; after becoming a Buddha, will I become deluded again? You need not worry. The Sutra of Perfect Enlightenment says: “It is like smelting gold ore: the gold is not there because of the smelting. Though it was originally gold, in the end it is perfected by smelting. Once it is the true gold substance, it never again becomes ore.” The “smelting” here is what we now call refining. Gold ore originally contains gold; it is not that refining produces the gold, because “the gold is not there because of the smelting.” This is a metaphor: sentient beings originally possess the Buddha-nature; it is not that they had no Buddha-nature and acquired it through cultivation. Yet though one is restoring the gold that was originally in the ore, in the end it is accomplished by means of smelting — “though it was originally gold, in the end it is perfected by smelting.” This is a metaphor: though sentient beings possess “original-enlightenment wisdom,” are fundamentally enlightened, yet because of delusive thinking and attachment they also possess ignorance and affliction; therefore they must practice and attain “initial-enlightenment wisdom,” and initial enlightenment joining original enlightenment, thus breaking ignorance and cutting off affliction, can the originally possessed Buddha-nature be opened and revealed. “Once it is the true gold substance, it never again becomes ore.” This is a metaphor: once one accomplishes the Way, one will never be deluded again.
Dharmatā, True Reality, Is the True Great Mudrā

blocks.text: 1. The Three Essentials of the Great Mudrā Are a Unified Whole

inline.s: “The three essentials of view, meditation, and action are the secret-meaning center of the Buddhas of the three times, the summit of all vehicles; therefore they are called the mother of all Buddhas.”

We said above: “View” is to understand the one true dharma-realm, the dharmatā tathāgatagarbha mind, which manifests immeasurably the dharmas of defilement and purity and is complete in the dharmatā’s meaning of equality. The “view school” alone is right knowledge and right view. “Meditation” is not dead concentration but living concentration; therefore only where emptiness and compassion are fused is there right concentration. “Action” is inwardly not to drift with deluded thoughts, outwardly not to be moved by states, to make the mind like a river, abiding spontaneously and naturally, guarding it in wakeful stillness and still wakefulness. This alone is right action. The three essentials are three key points. “The three essentials of view, meditation, and action are the secret-meaning center of the Buddhas of the three times”: the three times are the past, the present, and the future. The secret-meaning center of the Buddhas of the three times is the self-nature true suchness, the wondrous nirvāṇa mind, the one true dharma-realm, the wondrous luminous true mind, true suchness reality, the tathāgatagarbha mind, the great perfect-enlightenment ocean, suchness, bodhi, the dharma-body, the Buddha-nature, the dhāraṇī, the great Buddha-crown, the master within, the bottomless bowl, the stringless lute, the endless lamp, the rootless tree, the hair-splitting sword, the land of non-action, the maṇi jewel, the keyless lock — even the mud ox, the wooden horse, the mind-source, the mind-seal, the mind-mirror, the mind-moon, the mind-pearl, and so on. Though the names are many, the meaning is one. The “secret” of “secret meaning” means that it has no mark to be seen, cannot be spoken, has no dharma to be taught, and is not an object of language. It is not that it is deliberately kept secret and not told to people. Though it cannot be spoken, it is the center. This is the Mahāyāna Buddhist “seal of the one true mark,” by which one judges whether something is Mahāyāna Buddhism. If one departs from this purport and cannot speak to this point, it is not Mahāyāna Buddhism.

The Great Collection Sutra says: “In the dharma-ending age, of hundreds of millions of people who cultivate, scarcely one attains the Way; only by relying on Buddha-recitation can one cross over birth and death.” Nian, “to recite,” is the present mind — the single thought of the present moment. Fo, “Buddha,” is awakening — the true-suchness self-nature, the seal of the one true mark. The practice of the three essentials of view, meditation, and action makes the mind mindful of awakening in every thought, never apart from the seal of the one true mark; this is precisely “Buddha-recitation of true reality.” The Contemplation Sutra of Immeasurable Life sets forth sixteen contemplations; cultivating these sixteen contemplations is also Buddha-recitation, called “Buddha-recitation by contemplation,” and no contemplation departs from the wondrous luminous true mind. To gaze upon the holy marks of the Western Land of Ultimate Bliss and Amitābha Buddha, wondrous and adorned, to believe and rejoice with all one’s heart and vow to be born in that land, is also Buddha-recitation, called “Buddha-recitation of marks,” and it too never departs from the wondrous luminous true mind. To hold the holy name of Amitābha Buddha, mind reciting and ear hearing, gathering in the chaotic mind, transforming deluded thoughts into Buddha-thoughts, one phrase “Namo Amitābha Buddha” carried through from beginning to end, is called “Buddha-recitation of holding the name.” How could holding the name ever depart from the true mind by half a step! If the mouth recites but the mind does not practice, then it is not Buddha-recitation. Master Hanshan said: “The mouth recites Amitābha while the mind is scattered; you may shout your throat hoarse, and it is all in vain”! In the dharma-ending age, if one would cross over birth and death, one must rely on these various Buddha-recitation dharma-gates of “gathering in the six sense-faculties, pure mindfulness continuous.” The Great Mudrā is the most direct: it is precisely Buddha-recitation of true reality. It is precisely the secret-meaning center of the Buddhas of the three times.

The summit of all vehicles.” The esoteric school determines that Buddhadharma is divided into nine vehicles in sequence — the outer three vehicles, the inner three vehicles, and the esoteric three vehicles. The Ganges Great Mudrā and the Great Perfection both belong to the highest level, and so it is said that “the three essentials of view, meditation, and action” are the summit of all vehicles, like a pagoda reaching its topmost point. “Therefore they are called the mother of all Buddhas”: this is the mother of the Buddhas of the ten directions and three times; all Buddhas come into the world relying on this dharma, and all dharmas are derived from it.

“The above three essentials are the view, meditation, action, and fruit of the self-nature’s Great Perfection. The four, within the state of the self-nature’s thorough understanding, are gathered into one face — the utmost essential mind of practice. They are also the essential of meditation being just action.”

The view, meditation, action, and fruit of the self-nature’s Great Perfection” refers to the four stages of cultivating the self-nature’s Great Perfection. The above three essentials are the three essentials of right view, right meditation, and right action discussed above; they are the secret-meaning center of the Buddhas of the three times, that is, our own true-suchness nature. The purpose of cultivating the self-nature’s Great Perfection is to clarify the mind and see the nature, and to realize the fruit of Buddhahood. Without right view there is no right meditation; without right meditation there is no right action — where would right fruit come from? The sutra says: If the cause-ground is not right, the fruit is twisted. Therefore only with right view, right meditation, and right action can one realize and see the true-suchness Buddha-nature, and in the end become a Buddha. So it is said that the three essentials of view, meditation, and action are the view, meditation, action, and fruit of the self-nature’s Great Perfection.

The four” refers to the four stages of cultivation: first, establish the right view of liberation; then cultivate meditation to gather in and subdue the scattered mind; once the mind is settled, train amid affairs and states (the six pāramitās and ten thousand practices); and finally realize the fruit of Buddhahood. “The state of the self-nature’s thorough understanding” is the mind-state of “the self-nature’s Great Perfection.” In this mind-state, the four — view, meditation, action, and fruit — are gathered into one face, transformed into one body, and cannot be separated. This is the utmost essential mind of practice, the most crucial heart-essence and key point.

They are also the essential of meditation being just action”: action is meditation, meditation is action; meditation and action are one, and meditation and action cannot be separated. Not only are meditation and action thus; view, meditation, and action — all three — cannot be separated and must be fused into one body. For only when “view” is correct does one know what the great concentration that is neither entering nor emerging is, and not fall into dead concentration; only then does one know how to cultivate “effortless” action, avoid detours, and go straight to true suchness, in the end becoming a Buddha.
“That is, whenever one awakens to the bare wisdom-nature, at that very time one attains the view school of the self-nature’s wisdom.”

The bare wisdom-nature is our Buddha-nature: bare, clean, without form or mark, numinous and still-illuminating, without any covering. The Buddha-nature is great wisdom, the great wisdom that knows all and can do all. Whenever one can awaken to this bare wisdom-nature, at that very time one “attains the view school of the self-nature’s wisdom.” To attain the view school of the self-nature’s wisdom is to recognize the self-nature, to enter the great perfect mirror wisdom, to see the essential purport — that is, to clarify the mind and see the nature. After the view school, one will not seek outward, will not seek the Dharma outside the mind, and will not fall into non-Buddhist paths again. However great a superknowledge manifests on your side, on my side I do not waver in the least; my feet are planted firmly. If one has not realized to this degree, one’s footing is not firm and one cannot avoid wavering.

Long ago, at the foot of Mount Nanquan, there was a hermit. Someone told him: “Recently Chan Master Nanquan has come into the world; why not go and pay your respects?” Chan Master Nanquan has come forth to expound the Dharma and save beings — why do you not go and pay your respects? The hermit said: “Not only has Nanquan come into the world; even if a thousand Buddhas came forth, I would not go.” He meant that he had already recognized the original and his footing was firm; he would not waver. When Chan Master Nanquan heard of this, he sent his disciple Chan Master Zhaozhou to test him and see whether his feet truly touched the ground. Zhaozhou went and bowed to the hermit, but the hermit paid him no attention and sat motionless on his meditation bed. Zhaozhou walked from west to east and from east to west, and still the hermit paid him no attention. This hermit’s footing was settled: even if a living Buddha came into the world, I would pay him no attention. I have already recognized my own original face — utterly distinct, bare, clean, without a single thing. I am already awakened — what would I still seek? I am already sovereign in superknowledges; this freedom and ease is the great superknowledge. Everyone, take note: freedom and ease is the great superknowledge; it is not some strange and uncanny thing that is the great superknowledge. Zhaozhou had no way out; with a “clatter” he tore down the hermit’s curtain and said: “The straw thief is utterly defeated.” You dare not speak; you are not a true man but a straw thief; you have lost the great battle. Still the hermit paid him no attention, and Zhaozhou had no way out and had to return to the mountain defeated. Back on the mountain he told his master: this hermit has the Way; whatever I did, he did not move. Chan Master Nanquan said: “I have always suspected this fellow.” I long ago doubted whether his feet truly touched the ground. You did not stump him; let me go and test him. The next day Chan Master Nanquan took a novice, carrying a bottle of tea water and three teacups, and when he reached the hermitage he dashed them to the ground and said: “Yesterday’s, yesterday’s.” The hermit asked: “Yesterday’s — what is it?” Yesterday I was unmoved in suchness and your disciple was utterly helpless — what does that show? Now the fox’s tail is out: there is still a “what” to be explained! Chan Master Nanquan slapped the novice on the back and said: “He has tricked me, he has tricked me.” He shook his sleeves and returned. I have seen through you: there is still something there, you are still moved, your feet still have not touched the ground — you are still far short!

In our cultivation we must stand firm. Whatever qigong you have, whatever great superknowledges, if you are a non-Buddhist, I will not run after you. I cultivate the mind-ground method; I recognize the self-nature; in the future I will certainly realize the holy fruit. You do not know what the self-nature is; in the end you cannot realize the holy fruit. We once spoke of the case of Patriarch Lü Chunyang: he had already accomplished the yang spirit, yet Patriarch Huanglong said of him: “This corpse-guarding ghost.” Lü Chunyang said: “What of the elixir of long life in my bag?” “In the bag” means within the body. Did you not call me a corpse-guarding ghost? The corpse I guard — within the bag — holds the elixir of long life! This elixir refers to the “golden elixir” cultivated into being — the yang spirit. Patriarch Huanglong said: “Though you pass through eighty thousand kalpas, in the end you still fall into emptiness.” You will still fall into emptiness; you are merely longer-lived than others. The yang spirit is the body manifested by the seventh consciousness, the manas — called the mind-born body — false and unreal. Without recognizing the true mind, one still falls into emptiness. Having recognized the true mind, one is free and at ease, utterly unattached to marks. First attain the superknowledge of the extinction of defilements — the penetration of the Way. This alone is true penetration, the root. Having attained the penetration of the Way, you need not worry about not obtaining the five superknowledges; obtain the root and do not worry about the branches. This is very important; everyone must take note. That is: whenever one awakens to the bare wisdom-nature, at that very time one attains the view school of the self-nature’s wisdom.
“Though view and meditation are described separately, their essence is truly one.”

Though view and meditation are spoken of separately, they are not two but one body. What is called “view” is to recognize the original face; only with right knowledge and view does one know what the great concentration that is neither entering nor emerging is, and only then is there right concentration. Conversely, only when right concentration is attained is there right knowledge and view. Neither view nor meditation departs from our self-nature; both flow out from the self-nature. In essence, they are truly one thing. Not only are view and meditation “truly one in essence”; view, meditation, and action — all three — are also one body, none departing from our wondrous luminous true mind.

blocks.text: 2. The Great Mudrā Is the Essence of the Nine Vehicles of Buddhadharma

inline.s: “One who thus practices the flawless essential Way of the self-nature’s Great Perfection, originally pure, is truly at the summit of the nine vehicles.”

The self-nature’s Great Perfection” has already been explained above. “Originally pure”: the self-nature is originally perfect, originally pure. “The flawless essential Way”: the way of cultivation that is without error and of the utmost importance. “One who thus practices the flawless essential Way of the self-nature’s Great Perfection, originally pure” — how does one practice it? Exactly as described above in “the three essentials of view, meditation, and action.” First one must recognize the essence, and then cultivate from the essence. Understand that deluded thoughts and afflictions are precisely the essence’s wondrous function; neither run after them nor suppress them, but let them arise and cease of themselves, arising and ceasing vanishing with it. One need only recognize the essence and gather everything back into the essence. Practicing this “flawless essential Way” in this way — to deviate from this Way is to be flawed. Many who practice qigong have taken wrong turns and gone astray; this is of course losing the essential Way. Some who cultivate Chan do not know the correct method and get it wrong too, pursuing dead concentration until they become wood and stone; this too loses the essential Way. There are also those who cultivate the Pure Land wrongly: they use Buddha-recitation as copper coins, as banknotes, burning the Buddha-name like paper money to be deposited with King Yama, ready to collect after death. Is there such a Pure Land dharma-gate? There were many such people in the past, and not a few today. They are utterly mistaken. The Pure Land school is about rebirth in the Western Land of Ultimate Bliss — who told you to go to King Yama? Is this not turning things upside down! All of these have lost the essential Way.

One who practices this flawless essential Way “is truly at the summit of the nine vehicles.” When we spoke above of “the summit of all vehicles” we mentioned that the esoteric school divides Buddhadharma into nine vehicles in sequence — the outer three vehicles, the inner three vehicles, and the esoteric three vehicles. Let us now speak briefly of the content of these nine vehicles. The outer three vehicles are the śrāvaka vehicle, the pratyekabuddha vehicle, and the bodhisattva vehicle; they refer to the dharmas practiced by arhats, pratyekabuddhas, and bodhisattvas — the four noble truths, the twelvefold dependent origination, the six pāramitās and ten thousand practices, and so on — broadly meaning the exoteric teachings. The inner three vehicles refer to the cultivation methods of the three divisions: the action division, the performance division, and the yoga division. The action division is also called the service division, and includes such dharma-gates as increasing, pacifying, magnetizing, and subjugating. These are dharmas that arise in accord with beings’ wishes, expedient means of drawing beings in, “first hooking them with desire, then leading them into Buddha-wisdom”; they are not ultimate. The cultivation of the performance division aims at ending birth and death and escaping the sea of suffering, and only then does it count as entering true practice. It begins with visualization and cultivates the winds, channels, and drops, such as the phowa method and so on. Yoga means “correspondence”: in the yoga division’s cultivation, matters correspond with principle, words correspond with deeds, one corresponds with the Buddhas above and with beings below. From here three levels are opened, namely the esoteric three vehicles. The esoteric three vehicles are Mahāyoga, Anuyoga, and Atiyoga. Mahāyoga means “great-perfection correspondence”: the visualized winds, channels, and other mark-possessing things are dissolved into emptiness, to correspond with the markless dharma-body. Anuyoga means “unsurpassed-perfection correspondence”: taking the wisdom of the realm as the gate of entry, one further transforms all manifestations into the one true mark. Atiyoga means “incomparable-perfection correspondence”: one further unites the three vehicles into one great mantra vehicle. “One who thus practices the flawless essential Way of the self-nature’s Great Perfection, originally pure, is truly at the summit of the nine vehicles” — this is the supreme vehicle. The great mantra has no mantra to recite; the great mudrā has no mudrā to form. At this point, “nothing does not flow forth from this dharma-realm; nothing does not return to this dharma-realm,” and so it is called the “summit.”
“The ways of the remaining vehicles are merely followers, the platform and scaffolding and helpful companions of this essential Way.”

Since this flawless essential Way is the summit of the nine vehicles and the supreme vehicle, then “the ways of the remaining vehicles” — the other eight vehicles — “are merely followers, the platform and scaffolding and helpful companions of this essential Way”: the other various dharma-gates are merely followers, merely the platform and scaffolding and helpful companions of this essential Way. A platform is a step, merely a stairway for us to tread on as we climb to the top floor. Scaffolding is a frame: when we build a house we must put up a frame, but it is only used temporarily. “Helpful companions” are merely a help, merely an accompaniment, not the main practice. To accomplish the Way one must cultivate this “flawless essential Way”; other dharmas are merely platform and scaffolding and helpful companions. Without cultivating this mind-ground dharma-gate one cannot accomplish the Way. Without recognizing the true mind, how could one accomplish the Way? If one does not know that the true mind’s arising and manifesting of deluded thoughts is precisely wondrous function, does not know that deluded thoughts are precisely the true mind’s original-enlightenment wisdom marks, and only suppresses thoughts so they do not arise — even if one suppresses deluded thoughts to death, one still cannot accomplish the Way. But if one understands what deluded thoughts are, does not fear them, lets them arise and cease of themselves, arising and ceasing vanishing with it, and does not run after them — how relaxed this is, how joyful! The chest is no longer tight, the head no longer swollen, and in time one will certainly realize the great Way.
“When one sees the originally pure self-nature’s prajñā light, the function of the prajñā born of concentration blazes still more, like a summer waterfall.”

“Originally pure” means pure from the beginning. The self-nature’s prajñā light means the light manifested by the self-nature — prajñā, the great wisdom. It is not only the light seen when sitting in meditation; the light seen when sitting in meditation is bright light. But the “light” spoken of here does not necessarily mean bright light. All wondrous function is light: for example, when the mind turns and you think how this matter should be handled, how this person should be received — this too is light. One need not see a bright glow for it to be light; all wondrous function is the mark of wisdom-light. “When one sees the originally pure self-nature’s prajñā light,” when one sees the wisdom-light arising from the originally pure true-suchness Buddha-nature, at that time “the function of the prajñā born of concentration blazes still more”: the wondrous wisdom born of right concentration has an even vaster function. To blaze means to burn fiercely, like a flame burning violently. One may not even seek superknowledges, and superknowledges come of themselves. We said above: after recognizing the dharma-body, protect it and apply effort at every moment, do not run after deluded thoughts, do not follow states — this is concentration; at every moment and in every place constantly gathered in concentration, and in time wisdom is born of concentration and the function becomes even vaster, “like a summer waterfall”: like the cascading water of a summer waterfall. In summer the ice and snow melt and the water sources are abundant; add to that much rain, and so the waterfall’s flow is ceaseless and its momentum vast. This is a metaphor for prajñā-wisdom’s endless wondrous function.
“From the self-abiding of emptiness-nature, great compassion arises and enters boundless commiseration; this too is dharmatā.”

Dharma-nature, the Buddha-nature: its nature is fundamentally empty, and so it is called emptiness-nature. All things possess emptiness-nature and are unobtainable; this is called “nature is empty.” Its nature is empty; it is the nature of true emptiness. This emptiness-nature is originally unmoving, unshaking, neither born nor extinguished, neither coming nor going, neither increasing nor decreasing — this is called self-abiding. “From the self-abiding of emptiness-nature, great compassion arises”: one must give rise to the mind of great compassion; one must not only seek one’s own end of birth and death, but also save the vast multitude of beings. “Enter boundless commiseration”: boundless means without limit, infinitely vast. The commiseration of ordinary beings is small commiseration — commiseration for what? For one’s own children. My son, sweet darling, precious beyond words. Other people’s children — let them be, who cares. I support my own parents; other people’s parents — never mind, never mind! The scope of commiseration is far too small. Boundless commiseration means that whichever direction it may be, one has a mind of commiseration for beings in the worlds of the ten directions, and vows to save beings of the ten directions widely. “This too is dharmatā” — this is a matter of course. If one can accomplish the practice, one naturally enters boundless commiseration, and the mind of great compassion arises spontaneously. Some say arhats do not possess the mind of great compassion; in fact that is not so. That is one who has not yet realized the fourth fruit of arhatship; having reached the fourth fruit, he too spontaneously gives rise to the mind of great compassion. When he first aroused the mind, he regarded the three realms as a prison and looked on birth and death as an enemy. It is like some who cultivate the Pure Land today and say: “Once I reach the Western Land of Ultimate Bliss I will never come back, because this world is too bitter and too afflicted.” If one truly is born in the Western Land of Ultimate Bliss, one will still come back — why? Having heard the Buddhas and bodhisattvas of the Lotus Pool Assembly expound the great Dharma, one feels ashamed. To accomplish the Way one must save beings widely; without saving beings one cannot accomplish the Way! He too will “enter boundless commiseration; this too is dharmatā.” If one realizes the fourth fruit of arhatship and sees all the Buddhas and bodhisattvas delivering beings within the six paths, how can I sit here unmoving? One feels deeply ashamed. For example, if everyone in the same workplace is working and you alone sit there unmoving, are you not ashamed? Thereupon his mind of “unconditioned great loving-kindness, great compassion of one substance” arises spontaneously; this is called “turning from the small toward the great.” Turning from the small toward the great is likewise dharmatā.

“When the essential Way of the dual practice of emptiness-nature and great compassion is directly realized, all actions like the sea each manifest their function of themselves, like the sun and its light.”

If one truly realizes “emptiness-nature,” one no longer has the private feelings of ordinary beings. The feelings of ordinary beings are to care only for one’s own wife and children, and not for others at all. Once the mind is empty, prajñā’s great wisdom shines clearly before one, and the feelings of ordinary beings are utterly swept away. Being without feeling is great feeling, and the mind of great compassion naturally arises. This is “the dual practice of emptiness-nature and great compassion”; this is the “essential Way” — the key point of cultivating the Way, the key point of accomplishing the Way. Direct realization is to shine clearly before one. When this essential Way of the dual practice of emptiness and compassion shines clearly before one, “all actions like the sea each manifest their function of themselves.” The great sea is where a thousand rivers converge, and each river has its own different function. The Yangtze and the Yellow River have many tributaries too, and these small tributaries each have their own different function. Here boats can sail and transport; there irrigation can produce rice; elsewhere fish and shrimp abound. This is a metaphor: when we realize emptiness-nature and then give rise to great compassion everywhere, delivering beings within the six paths of transmigration, at every moment and in every place different wondrous actions can manifest. “Like the sun and its light”: they are as inseparable as the sun and its light. Only with the sun is there light, and only then do you see things; without the sun you are in darkness and see nothing. The relation between emptiness-nature and great compassion is as inseparable as the relation between the sun and its light: only with the sun is there light; without the sun where would light come from? The sun is a metaphor for emptiness-nature, light a metaphor for great compassion; the two are closely joined and inseparable.
“Thus, working together with the provisions of merit, one widely performs the practices that benefit others, so as to perfect the true view school and become the companion of undefiled still bliss.”

To realize emptiness-nature is to possess wisdom; to give rise to great compassion is to possess merit. Only by widely saving beings and serving beings is there merit. If there is only wisdom and no merit, or if the provisions of merit are insufficient, one cannot become a Buddha. For a Buddha is the “doubly honored one,” complete in wisdom and complete in merit. Therefore we must cultivate both merit and wisdom; to cultivate only wisdom and emptiness, not merit, not doing things for beings, merit is not perfected and one cannot perfect the fruit of Buddhahood. An arhat’s resolve is small: he cares only for his own liberation, does not save beings, does not serve beings, and so possesses wisdom but not merit; therefore he cannot become a Buddha, and he will certainly “turn from the small toward the great.” “Thus, working together with the provisions of merit”: provisions are capital, and grain is the grain of the Way; the provisions for accomplishing the Way are like the travel funds for a journey, indispensable. Therefore one must certainly arouse the great mind, arouse bodhicitta, and cultivate both merit and wisdom, and only then can one perfect the fruit of Buddhahood. The great bodhisattva’s first arousal of the mind is for the sake of widely saving beings; he says: I study Buddhism not for myself but for beings. For example, if beings are drowning in the great sea and about to die, I want to save them, but I cannot swim and do not know lifesaving; how then can I save them? My studying Buddhism for self-liberation is first learning to swim and learning lifesaving. Once I have learned it and my skills are great, I will go and save beings. Self-liberation is only the means; saving beings is the goal. To study Buddhism for beings, not for oneself — this is the bodhisattva of the great mind. If one arouses the small mind, seeking only to leap out of birth-and-death transmigration for oneself, then one can only accomplish the fruit of arhatship and cannot be called a bodhisattva. This is the difference between the Mahāyāna bodhisattva and the Hīnayāna sage.

To realize the emptiness-nature of wisdom and to work together with the provisions of merit from widely saving beings is to “widely perform the practices that benefit others.” “Widely” means to do a great deal, not a little. The practices that benefit others are matters beneficial to beings; one must do many things beneficial to beings. To do one good deed is easy enough, but to do it for a long time is hard, and to do it every day without interruption is harder still. Take illumination: to illuminate for a time is very easy, but never to forget it at any moment is very hard. Yet nothing in the world is difficult for one who sets his heart to it. If you can illuminate continuously for seven days, never forgetting at any moment during those seven days, then afterward it will not be difficult. The Amitābha Sutra says: “Whether for one day, or two days, or three, four, five, six, or seven days, with one mind undistracted, when such a person approaches the end of life, Amitābha Buddha and all the holy assembly will appear before him.” If one can be mindful without forgetting for seven days, afterward one will not easily forget. To widely perform the practices that benefit others is to do many things beneficial to beings over a long time, to be willing to sacrifice oneself and help others, “so as to perfect the true view school and become the companion of undefiled still bliss.” Use “widely performing the practices that benefit others” to perfectly accomplish “the true view school,” to truly perfect the essential purport you have seen. Let us explain “still bliss”: only when even bliss is unobtainable is it called still bliss. If there is still bliss in it, that is ruinous, for bliss and suffering are relative; where there is bliss there is suffering, and suffering is within bliss. Still bliss: bliss too is unobtainable — how could there be suffering? The “Land of Ultimate Bliss” is bliss taken to its utmost, where bliss too is unobtainable. Worldly dhyāna is like this too: the second dhyāna is joy, the third dhyāna is bliss, and by the fourth dhyāna, the “ground of pure renunciation of thought,” bliss too is unobtainable and all is pure. “Undefiled still bliss” is still bliss that has never been defiled; this is precisely the wondrous luminous true mind, the one true dharma-realm, the great perfect-enlightenment ocean. To make “widely performing the practices that benefit others” the companion of “undefiled still bliss” is great compassion accompanying emptiness-nature, the six pāramitās and ten thousand practices accompanying prajñā-wisdom. We have spoken above at length of how to practice in order to open wisdom; but opening wisdom alone is not enough — one must also “widely perform the practices that benefit others” and cultivate merit. There are many practices that benefit others; we will not speak of them in detail here. We must do our utmost to help beings: if you have money, give money; if you have strength, give strength; exhaust what you are capable of. Even if you can help others merely by saying a kind word, that too is good.

blocks.text: 3. A Summary of the Three Essentials of the Great Mudrā

inline.s: “The three essentials are: to know the marks of one’s own mind; relying on deluded thoughts’ conditioning by states and the arising of thoughts with them, to observe the original marks of one’s own mind; and to recognize the dharma-body’s self-nature (this is view).”
The three essentials are the three essentials of view, meditation, and action. This passage speaks of “view.”
